docs.title: Complex Network Dynamics
docs.text:
Python toolkit for complex networks of nonlinear oscillators: simulate maps and ODE networks, compute Lyapunov spectra and synchronisation, and infer network structure from time series.

Get started Tutorials GitHub

docs.title: From dynamics to networks
docs.text:
• Simulate

    Run dynamics on a network and keep the node time series.

    • Discrete models: logistic and circle maps, coupled-map networks
    • Continuous models: Lorenz, Rössler, Hindmarsh–Rose, Kuramoto (also stochastic), Lotka–Volterra
    • Integrators: Euler, RK4, SciPy and compiled RK4
    • Datasets: example adjacency matrices

  • Analyse

    Measure the stability and the collective behaviour of the network.

    • Lyapunov spectra, computed alongside the integration
    • Synchronisation: Hilbert phases, Kuramoto order parameter, phase locking
    • Network metrics: diameter and average path length

  • Infer

    Recover the network from the time series alone.

    • Network inference: Mutual Information Rate (MIR)
    • Surrogate data: amplitude-phase modulated surrogates (APMSD)
    • A false-discovery-rate test that decides which links are real

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Requires Python 3.10–3.13. From the project root:

pip install -e .

Dependencies: numpy, scipy, matplotlib, numba, networkx.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from complex_network_dynamics import (
    load_network, logistic, df_logistic, simulate_discrete_models, MIR, plot_similarity_gap_bars,
)

# 1. Load a network
A = load_network("16nodes")

# 2. Simulate coupled logistic maps on it
traj, lyap = simulate_discrete_models(np.random.rand(16), logistic, df_logistic, A, t=10_000, alpha=0.1)

# 3. Infer the network back from the time series
mir, mi = MIR(traj)
plot_similarity_gap_bars(mir, A)

docs.title: Lorenz system
docs.text:
\[ \dot x = \sigma (y - x), \qquad \dot y = x(\rho - z) - y, \qquad \dot z = x y - \beta z \]

Defaults \(\sigma = 10\), \(\rho = 28\), \(\beta = 8/3\) give the chaotic Lorenz attractor.

docs.title: Coupled Lorenz network
docs.text:
\(N\) Lorenz oscillators are coupled diffusively through \(x\), with adjacency matrix \(A\) and strength \(K\):

\[ \dot x_i = \sigma (y_i - x_i) + K \sum_j A_{ij}\,(x_j - x_i) \]

The state is a blocked vector of length \(3N\): \([x_1,\dots,x_N,\; y_1,\dots,y_N,\; z_1,\dots,z_N]\).

import numpy as np
from complex_network_dynamics import load_network, coupled_lorenz, coupled_lorenz_jacobian, rk4_with_lyapunov

A = load_network("12nodes")
y0 = np.random.rand(3 * A.shape[0])

t, traj, spectrum = rk4_with_lyapunov(
    coupled_lorenz, y0, t0=0.0, h=0.01, n_steps=20_000,
    df=coupled_lorenz_jacobian, A=A, K=0.5,
)

docs.title: Lotka–Volterra
docs.text:
\[ \dot x = \alpha x - \beta x p, \qquad \dot p = \delta x p - \gamma p \]

with \(x\) the prey and \(p\) the predator population.

docs.title: Kuramoto oscillators
docs.text:
\[ \dot\theta_i = \omega_i + \frac{K}{M}\sum_j A_{ij}\sin(\theta_j - \theta_i) \]

stochastic_kuramoto adds independent noise of strength \(D\), \(d\theta_i = [\dots]\,dt + D\,dW_i\), and integrates it with Euler–Maruyama, as in the thesis (defaults \(K = D = 10\)).

from complex_network_dynamics import load_network, stochastic_kuramoto

# theta0: initial phases, w: natural frequencies, both shape (16,)
t, phases = stochastic_kuramoto(theta0, load_network("16nodes"), w, K=10, D=10, dt=0.1, n_steps=50_000, rng=0)

docs.title: Rössler oscillators
docs.text:
Coupled through \(x\), with a frequency \(\omega_i\) per node:

\[ \dot x_i = -\omega_i y_i - z_i + K\sum_j A_{ij}(x_j - x_i), \qquad \dot y_i = \omega_i x_i + a y_i, \qquad \dot z_i = f + z_i(x_i - c) \]

docs.title: Hindmarsh–Rose neurons
docs.text:
Coupled through the membrane potential \(p\) with the graph Laplacian \(C = D - A\):

\[ \dot p_i = q_i - p_i^3 + 3p_i^2 - n_i + 3.25 - g\sum_l C_{il}\,p_l, \qquad \dot q_i = 1 - 5p_i^2 - q_i, \qquad \dot n_i = 0.02(p_i + 1.6) - 0.005\,n_i \]

All Jacobians are checked against finite differences.

def lorenz(t, y, sigma=10.0, rho=28.0, beta=8.0 / 3.0):
    """Lorenz system.

        dx/dt = sigma (y - x)
        dy/dt = x (rho - z) - y
        dz/dt = x y - beta z

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused).
    y : array_like
        State [x, y, z].
    sigma : float, optional
        Prandtl number. Default is 10.0.
    rho : float, optional
        Rayleigh number. Default is 28.0.
    beta : float, optional
        Geometric factor. Default is 8/3.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        [dx/dt, dy/dt, dz/dt] with shape (3,).

    See Also
    --------
    lorenz_njit : Numba-compiled version for `build_rk4_lyapunov`, about 10 times faster.
    """
    x, y_coord, z = y
    dxdt = sigma * (y_coord - x)
    dydt = x * (rho - z) - y_coord
    dzdt = x * y_coord - beta * z
    return np.array([dxdt, dydt, dzdt])

def lorenz_jacobian(t, y, sigma=10.0, rho=28.0, beta=8.0 / 3.0):
    """Jacobian of the Lorenz system.

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused).
    y : array_like
        State [x, y, z].
    sigma : float, optional
        Prandtl number. Default is 10.0.
    rho : float, optional
        Rayleigh number. Default is 28.0.
    beta : float, optional
        Geometric factor. Default is 8/3.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Jacobian matrix of shape (3, 3).

    See Also
    --------
    lorenz_jacobian_njit : Numba-compiled version for `build_rk4_lyapunov`.
    """
    x, y_coord, z = y
    return np.array(
        [[-sigma, sigma, 0.0], [rho - z, -1.0, -x], [y_coord, x, -beta]]
    )

docs.text:
coupled_lorenz(
    t, y, A, K=0.1, sigma=10.0, rho=28.0, beta=8.0 / 3.0
)

Network of diffusively coupled Lorenz oscillators.

Nodes are coupled through the x variable:

dx_i/dt = sigma (y_i - x_i) + K sum_j A_ij (x_j - x_i)
dy_i/dt = x_i (rho - z_i) - y_i
dz_i/dt = x_i y_i - beta z_i

This is Eq. (20) of Yildirim & Antonopoulos (2024), which uses K = 0.2.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default t float

Time (unused).

required y array_like

Blocked state vector of length 3N: [x_1..x_N, y_1..y_N, z_1..z_N].

required A array_like

Adjacency matrix of shape (N, N). A[i, j] is the weight of the link from node j to node i: row i lists the nodes that drive node i.

required K float

Coupling strength. Default is 0.1.

0.1 sigma float

Prandtl number. Default is 10.0.

10.0 rho float

Rayleigh number. Default is 28.0.

28.0 beta float

Geometric factor. Default is 8/3.

8.0 / 3.0

def coupled_lorenz(t, y, A, K=0.1, sigma=10.0, rho=28.0, beta=8.0 / 3.0):
    """Network of diffusively coupled Lorenz oscillators.

    Nodes are coupled through the x variable:

        dx_i/dt = sigma (y_i - x_i) + K sum_j A_ij (x_j - x_i)
        dy_i/dt = x_i (rho - z_i) - y_i
        dz_i/dt = x_i y_i - beta z_i

    This is Eq. (20) of Yildirim & Antonopoulos (2024), which uses K = 0.2.

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused).
    y : array_like
        Blocked state vector of length 3N: [x_1..x_N, y_1..y_N, z_1..z_N].
    A : array_like
        Adjacency matrix of shape (N, N). A[i, j] is the weight of the link
        from node j to node i: row i lists the nodes that drive node i.
    K : float, optional
        Coupling strength. Default is 0.1.
    sigma : float, optional
        Prandtl number. Default is 10.0.
    rho : float, optional
        Rayleigh number. Default is 28.0.
    beta : float, optional
        Geometric factor. Default is 8/3.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Blocked derivative vector of length 3N.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If the size of `y` is not 3N.

    See Also
    --------
    coupled_lorenz_njit : Numba-compiled version for `build_rk4_lyapunov`.
    """
    y_flat = np.asarray(y, dtype=float).ravel()
    A_mat = np.asarray(A, dtype=float)

    N = A_mat.shape[0]
    if y_flat.size != 3 * N:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Dimension mismatch: A is ({N}, {N}) expecting 3*N={3*N} states, but got y of size {y_flat.size}"
        )

    # 1. Unpack blocked components: [x_all, y_all, z_all]
    x = y_flat[0:N]
    y_coord = y_flat[N : 2 * N]
    z = y_flat[2 * N : 3 * N]

    # Diffusive coupling term: K * sum_j A_ij (x_j - x_i)
    degrees = np.asarray(A_mat.sum(axis=1)).ravel()
    coupling_x = K * (A_mat @ x - degrees * x)

    # Compute node derivatives
    dxdt = sigma * (y_coord - x) + coupling_x
    dydt_nodes = x * (rho - z) - y_coord
    dzdt = x * y_coord - beta * z

    # 2. Return as blocked 1D vector: [dx, dy, dz]
    return np.concatenate([dxdt, dydt_nodes, dzdt])

def coupled_lorenz_jacobian(
    t, y, A, K=0.1, sigma=10.0, rho=28.0, beta=8.0 / 3.0
):
    """Jacobian of the coupled Lorenz network.

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused).
    y : array_like
        Blocked state vector of length 3N: [x_1..x_N, y_1..y_N, z_1..z_N].
    A : array_like
        Adjacency matrix of shape (N, N), with the convention of
        `coupled_lorenz`.
    K : float, optional
        Coupling strength. Default is 0.1.
    sigma : float, optional
        Prandtl number. Default is 10.0.
    rho : float, optional
        Rayleigh number. Default is 28.0.
    beta : float, optional
        Geometric factor. Default is 8/3.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Jacobian matrix of shape (3N, 3N).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If the size of `y` is not 3N.

    See Also
    --------
    coupled_lorenz_jacobian_njit : Numba-compiled version for `build_rk4_lyapunov`.
    """
    y_flat = np.asarray(y, dtype=float).ravel()
    A_mat = np.asarray(A, dtype=float)

    N = A_mat.shape[0]
    if y_flat.size != 3 * N:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Dimension mismatch: A is ({N}, {N}) expecting 3*N={3*N} states, but got y of size {y_flat.size}"
        )
    x = y_flat[0:N]
    y_coord = y_flat[N : 2 * N]
    z = y_flat[2 * N : 3 * N]

    degrees = np.asarray(A_mat.sum(axis=1)).ravel()

    # Allocate full 3N x 3N Jacobian
    J = np.zeros((3 * N, 3 * N), dtype=float)

    # Slice indices:
    # x-block: [0 : N], y-block: [N : 2N], z-block: [2N : 3N]

    # dx/dx block: -sigma * I + coupling
    J[0:N, 0:N] = K * A_mat - np.diag(sigma + K * degrees)

    # dx/dy block: sigma * I
    J[0:N, N : 2 * N] = sigma * np.eye(N)

    # dy/dx block: diag(rho - z)
    J[N : 2 * N, 0:N] = np.diag(rho - z)

    # dy/dy block: -I
    J[N : 2 * N, N : 2 * N] = -np.eye(N)

    # dy/dz block: diag(-x)
    J[N : 2 * N, 2 * N : 3 * N] = np.diag(-x)

    # dz/dx block: diag(y_coord)
    J[2 * N : 3 * N, 0:N] = np.diag(y_coord)

    # dz/dy block: diag(x)
    J[2 * N : 3 * N, N : 2 * N] = np.diag(x)

    # dz/dz block: -beta * I
    J[2 * N : 3 * N, 2 * N : 3 * N] = -beta * np.eye(N)

    return J

docs.text:
lotka_volterra(
    t, y, alpha=1.1, beta=0.4, delta=0.1, gamma=0.4
)

Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model.

dx/dt = alpha x - beta x p
dp/dt = delta x p - gamma p

The orbits are closed curves around the equilibrium (gamma/delta, alpha/beta), on which V = delta x - gamma ln x + beta p - alpha ln p stays constant, so the system is not chaotic and both Lyapunov exponents are zero.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default t float

Time (unused).

required y array_like

State [x, p]: y[0] is the prey, y[1] the predator population.

required alpha float

Prey growth rate. Default is 1.1.

1.1 beta float

Predation rate. Default is 0.4.

0.4 delta float

Predator growth per prey eaten. Default is 0.1.

0.1 gamma float

Predator death rate. Default is 0.4.

0.4

[dx/dt, dp/dt].

def lotka_volterra(t, y, alpha=1.1, beta=0.4, delta=0.1, gamma=0.4):
    """Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model.

        dx/dt = alpha x - beta x p
        dp/dt = delta x p - gamma p

    The orbits are closed curves around the equilibrium (gamma/delta, alpha/beta),
    on which V = delta x - gamma ln x + beta p - alpha ln p stays constant, so
    the system is not chaotic and both Lyapunov exponents are zero.

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused).
    y : array_like
        State [x, p]: y[0] is the prey, y[1] the predator population.
    alpha : float, optional
        Prey growth rate. Default is 1.1.
    beta : float, optional
        Predation rate. Default is 0.4.
    delta : float, optional
        Predator growth per prey eaten. Default is 0.1.
    gamma : float, optional
        Predator death rate. Default is 0.4.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        [dx/dt, dp/dt].
    """
    x, p = y[0], y[1]
    dxdt = alpha * x - beta * x * p
    dpdt = delta * x * p - gamma * p
    return np.array([dxdt, dpdt])

def lotka_volterra_jacobian(
    t, y, alpha=1.1, beta=0.4, delta=0.1, gamma=0.4):
    """Jacobian matrix of the 2D Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model.

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused).
    y : array_like
        State [x, p]: y[0] is the prey, y[1] the predator population.
    alpha, beta, delta, gamma : float, optional
        Model parameters, as in `lotka_volterra`.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Jacobian matrix of shape (2, 2).
    """
    x, p = y[0], y[1]

    df1_dx = alpha - beta * p
    df1_dp = -beta * x
    df2_dx = delta * p
    df2_dp = delta * x - gamma

    return np.array([[df1_dx, df1_dp], [df2_dx, df2_dp]], dtype=float)

def kuramoto(t, y, A, w, K=1.0):
    """Kuramoto oscillators on a network.

        dtheta_i/dt = w_i + (K / M) sum_j A_ij sin(theta_j - theta_i)

    This is Eq. (22) of Yildirim & Antonopoulos (2024).

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused).
    y : array_like
        Phases theta_1..theta_M.
    A : array_like
        Adjacency matrix, shape (M, M). A[i, j] is the weight of the link
        from node j to node i: row i lists the nodes that drive node i.
    w : array_like
        Natural frequencies, shape (M,).
    K : float, optional
        Coupling strength. Default is 1.0.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        dtheta/dt, shape (M,).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `A` is not (M, M) or `w` does not have M entries.

    See Also
    --------
    stochastic_kuramoto : The same model with noise, Eq. (23) of the paper.
    """
    theta, A, w = _kuramoto_inputs(y, A, w)
    diff = theta[None, :] - theta[:, None]  # theta_j - theta_i
    return w + (K / len(theta)) * np.sum(A * np.sin(diff), axis=1)

def kuramoto_jacobian(t, y, A, w, K=1.0):
    """Jacobian of `kuramoto`.

    J_ij = (K / M) A_ij cos(theta_j - theta_i) for i != j, and each diagonal
    entry is minus the sum of the other entries in its row.

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused).
    y : array_like
        Phases theta_1..theta_M.
    A : array_like
        Adjacency matrix, shape (M, M), with the convention of `kuramoto`.
    w : array_like
        Natural frequencies, shape (M,). They do not enter the Jacobian.
    K : float, optional
        Coupling strength. Default is 1.0.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Jacobian matrix of shape (M, M).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `A` is not (M, M) or `w` does not have M entries.
    """
    theta, A, w = _kuramoto_inputs(y, A, w)
    M = len(theta)
    J = (K / M) * A * np.cos(theta[None, :] - theta[:, None])
    np.fill_diagonal(J, 0.0)  # a self-loop adds sin(0), which has zero derivative
    J -= np.diag(J.sum(axis=1))
    return J

def stochastic_kuramoto(theta0, A, w, K=10.0, D=10.0, dt=0.1, n_steps=1000, rng=None):
    """Stochastic Kuramoto oscillators, integrated with Euler-Maruyama.

        dtheta_i = [w_i + (K / M) sum_j A_ij sin(theta_j - theta_i)] dt + D dW_i

    with independent Wiener processes W_i. This is Eq. (3.18) of the thesis
    and Eq. (23) of Yildirim & Antonopoulos (2024), integrated with the
    Euler-Maruyama scheme. The defaults K = D = 10 are those of the thesis,
    which draws w_i uniformly in [-pi, pi]; the paper uses K = 4, D = 0.05
    and states w_i in [-2 pi, 2 pi].

    Parameters
    ----------
    theta0 : array_like
        Initial phases, shape (M,).
    A : array_like
        Adjacency matrix, shape (M, M), with the convention of `kuramoto`.
    w : array_like
        Natural frequencies, shape (M,).
    K : float, optional
        Coupling strength. Default is 10, as in the thesis.
    D : float, optional
        Noise strength. Default is 10, as in the thesis.
    dt : float, optional
        Time step. Default is 0.1.
    n_steps : int, optional
        Number of steps. Default is 1000.
    rng : numpy.random.Generator or int, optional
        Random generator or seed.

    Returns
    -------
    t : np.ndarray
        Times, shape (n_steps + 1,).
    phases : np.ndarray
        Phases (not wrapped), shape (n_steps + 1, M); the first row is theta0.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `A` is not (M, M) or `w` does not have M entries.

    See Also
    --------
    kuramoto : The deterministic model, Eq. (22) of the paper.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(rng)
    theta, A, w = _kuramoto_inputs(theta0, A, w)
    theta = theta.copy()
    phases = np.empty((n_steps + 1, len(theta)))
    phases[0] = theta
    noise = D * np.sqrt(dt) * rng.standard_normal((n_steps, len(theta)))
    for k in range(n_steps):
        theta = theta + kuramoto(0.0, theta, A, w, K) * dt + noise[k]
        phases[k + 1] = theta
    return dt * np.arange(n_steps + 1), phases

def rossler(t, y, A, K=0.1, w=1.0, a=0.2, f=0.2, c=5.7):
    """Rossler oscillators coupled through x.

        dx_i/dt = -w_i y_i - z_i + K sum_j A_ij (x_j - x_i)
        dy_i/dt =  w_i x_i + a y_i
        dz_i/dt =  f + z_i (x_i - c)

    This is `rossler_ext` of the thesis MATLAB code.

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused).
    y : array_like
        Blocked state vector of length 3M: [x_1..x_M, y_1..y_M, z_1..z_M].
    A : array_like
        Adjacency matrix, shape (M, M). A[i, j] is the weight of the link
        from node j to node i: row i lists the nodes that drive node i.
    K : float, optional
        Coupling strength. Default is 0.1.
    w : float or array_like, optional
        Frequency of each oscillator: one value for all, or M values.
        Default is 1.0.
    a, f, c : float, optional
        Rossler parameters. Defaults are 0.2, 0.2 and 5.7.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Blocked derivative vector of length 3M.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `y` does not have 3M entries or `w` has neither 1 nor M entries.
    """
    s, A, w, M = _rossler_inputs(y, A, w)
    x, yy, z = s[:M], s[M:2 * M], s[2 * M:]
    coupling = K * (A @ x - A.sum(axis=1) * x)
    return np.concatenate([-w * yy - z + coupling, w * x + a * yy, f + z * (x - c)])

def rossler_jacobian(t, y, A, K=0.1, w=1.0, a=0.2, f=0.2, c=5.7):
    """Jacobian of `rossler`.

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused).
    y : array_like
        Blocked state vector of length 3M: [x_1..x_M, y_1..y_M, z_1..z_M].
    A : array_like
        Adjacency matrix, shape (M, M), with the convention of `rossler`.
    K : float, optional
        Coupling strength. Default is 0.1.
    w : float or array_like, optional
        Frequency of each oscillator: one value for all, or M values.
        Default is 1.0.
    a, f, c : float, optional
        Rossler parameters. Defaults are 0.2, 0.2 and 5.7.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Jacobian matrix of shape (3M, 3M).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `y` does not have 3M entries or `w` has neither 1 nor M entries.
    """
    s, A, w, M = _rossler_inputs(y, A, w)
    x, z = s[:M], s[2 * M:]
    I = np.eye(M)
    J = np.zeros((3 * M, 3 * M))
    J[:M, :M] = K * A - np.diag(K * A.sum(axis=1))
    J[:M, M:2 * M] = -np.diag(w)
    J[:M, 2 * M:] = -I
    J[M:2 * M, :M] = np.diag(w)
    J[M:2 * M, M:2 * M] = a * I
    J[2 * M:, :M] = np.diag(z)
    J[2 * M:, 2 * M:] = np.diag(x - c)
    return J

def hindmarsh_rose(t, y, A, g=0.1, a=1.0, b=3.0, c=1.0, d=5.0, r=0.005, s=4.0, p0=-1.6, I_ext=3.25):
    """Hindmarsh-Rose neurons coupled through the membrane potential.

        dp_i/dt = q_i - a p_i^3 + b p_i^2 - n_i + I_ext - g sum_l C_il p_l
        dq_i/dt = c - d p_i^2 - q_i
        dn_i/dt = r (s (p_i - p0) - n_i)

    where C = D - A is the graph Laplacian and D the diagonal matrix of the
    row sums of A, so the coupling is g * sum_l A_il (p_l - p_i). This is
    Eq. (21) of Yildirim & Antonopoulos (2024) and Eq. (3.14) of the thesis,
    as computed by the thesis MATLAB code (`HR_ext`). The paper and thesis
    print C = A - D and r = 0.05 (called h there); the code uses C = D - A
    and r = 0.005, the values used here.

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused).
    y : array_like
        Blocked state vector of length 3M: [p_1..p_M, q_1..q_M, n_1..n_M].
    A : array_like
        Adjacency matrix, shape (M, M). A[i, j] is the weight of the link
        from node j to node i: row i lists the nodes that drive node i.
    g : float, optional
        Coupling strength. Default is 0.1.
    a, b, c, d : float, optional
        Parameters of the fast subsystem. Defaults are 1, 3, 1 and 5.
    r : float, optional
        Time scale of the slow current n (h in the paper). Default is 0.005.
    s, p0 : float, optional
        Adaptation strength and resting potential. Defaults are 4 and -1.6.
    I_ext : float, optional
        External current. Default is 3.25, which gives chaotic bursting.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Blocked derivative vector of length 3M.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `A` is not square or `y` does not have 3M entries.
    """
    state, C, M = _hindmarsh_rose_inputs(y, A)
    p, q, n = state[:M], state[M:2 * M], state[2 * M:]
    return np.concatenate([
        q - a * p**3 + b * p**2 - n + I_ext - g * (C @ p),
        c - d * p**2 - q,
        r * (s * (p - p0) - n),
    ])

def hindmarsh_rose_jacobian(t, y, A, g=0.1, a=1.0, b=3.0, c=1.0, d=5.0, r=0.005, s=4.0, p0=-1.6, I_ext=3.25):
    """Jacobian of `hindmarsh_rose`.

    The entry dp/dp is -3 a p^2 + 2 b p - g C, the derivative of the vector
    field (with the defaults, -3 p^2 + 6 p - g C).

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused).
    y : array_like
        Blocked state vector of length 3M: [p_1..p_M, q_1..q_M, n_1..n_M].
    A : array_like
        Adjacency matrix, shape (M, M), with the convention of `hindmarsh_rose`.
    g, a, b, c, d, r, s, p0, I_ext : float, optional
        Model parameters, as in `hindmarsh_rose`. c, p0 and I_ext do not
        enter the Jacobian.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Jacobian matrix of shape (3M, 3M).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `A` is not square or `y` does not have 3M entries.
    """
    state, C, M = _hindmarsh_rose_inputs(y, A)
    p = state[:M]
    I = np.eye(M)
    J = np.zeros((3 * M, 3 * M))
    J[:M, :M] = np.diag(-3 * a * p**2 + 2 * b * p) - g * C
    J[:M, M:2 * M] = I
    J[:M, 2 * M:] = -I
    J[M:2 * M, :M] = np.diag(-2 * d * p)
    J[M:2 * M, M:2 * M] = -I
    J[2 * M:, :M] = r * s * I
    J[2 * M:, 2 * M:] = -r * I
    return J

@njit
def lorenz_njit(t, y, args):
    """Lorenz vector field, compiled with Numba.

    Use with `build_rk4_lyapunov`.

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused; the system is autonomous).
    y : np.ndarray
        State [x, y, z].
    args : tuple
        (sigma, rho, beta).

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Flat array [dx/dt, dy/dt, dz/dt] of shape (3,).

    See Also
    --------
    lorenz : The same system in plain Python, with keyword parameters.
    """
    sigma, rho, beta = args
    x, y_coord, z = y

    dxdt = sigma * (y_coord - x)
    dydt = x * (rho - z) - y_coord
    dzdt = x * y_coord - beta * z

    # Must return a flat 1D array, no .reshape((1,3))
    return np.array([dxdt, dydt, dzdt], dtype=np.float64)

        dx_i/dt = sigma (y_i - x_i) + K sum_j A_ij (x_j - x_i)
        dy_i/dt = x_i (rho - z_i) - y_i
        dz_i/dt = x_i y_i - beta z_i

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused).
    y : np.ndarray
        Blocked state vector of length 3N: [x_1..x_N, y_1..y_N, z_1..z_N].
    args : tuple
        (A_mat, K, sigma, rho, beta), where A_mat is the (N, N) adjacency
        matrix, with the convention of `coupled_lorenz`, and K the coupling
        strength. A_mat must be a float array: an integer matrix fails to
        compile, so pass `A.astype(float)`.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Blocked derivative vector of length 3N.

    See Also
    --------
    coupled_lorenz : The same system in plain Python, with keyword parameters.
    """
    A_mat, K, sigma, rho, beta = args
    N = A_mat.shape[0]

    # Unpack blocked components: [x_all, y_all, z_all]
    x = y[0:N]
    y_coord = y[N : 2 * N]
    z = y[2 * N : 3 * N]

    # Diffusive coupling term
    degrees = np.sum(A_mat, axis=1)
    coupling_x = K * (A_mat @ x - degrees * x)

    # Compute node derivatives
    dxdt = sigma * (y_coord - x) + coupling_x
    dydt_nodes = x * (rho - z) - y_coord
    dzdt = x * y_coord - beta * z

    # Fast Numba array construction (avoids np.concatenate overhead)
    dy = np.empty(3 * N, dtype=np.float64)
    dy[0:N] = dxdt
    dy[N:2*N] = dydt_nodes
    dy[2*N:3*N] = dzdt

    return dy

@njit
def coupled_lorenz_jacobian_njit(t, y, args):
    """Jacobian of the coupled Lorenz network, compiled with Numba.

    Parameters
    ----------
    t : float
        Time (unused).
    y : np.ndarray
        Blocked state vector of length 3N.
    args : tuple
        (A_mat, K, sigma, rho, beta), as in `coupled_lorenz_njit`; A_mat
        must be a float array.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Jacobian matrix of shape (3N, 3N).

    See Also
    --------
    coupled_lorenz_jacobian : The same Jacobian in plain Python, with keyword parameters.
    """
    A_mat, K, sigma, rho, beta = args
    N = A_mat.shape[0]

    x = y[0:N]
    y_coord = y[N : 2 * N]
    z = y[2 * N : 3 * N]

    degrees = np.sum(A_mat, axis=1)

    # Allocate full 3N x 3N Jacobian
    J = np.zeros((3 * N, 3 * N), dtype=np.float64)

    # dx/dx block: -sigma * I + coupling
    J[0:N, 0:N] = K * A_mat - np.diag(sigma + K * degrees)

    # dx/dy block: sigma * I
    J[0:N, N : 2 * N] = sigma * np.eye(N)

    # dy/dx block: diag(rho - z)
    J[N : 2 * N, 0:N] = np.diag(rho - z)

    # dy/dy block: -I
    J[N : 2 * N, N : 2 * N] = -np.eye(N)

    # dy/dz block: diag(-x)
    J[N : 2 * N, 2 * N : 3 * N] = np.diag(-x)

    # dz/dx block: diag(y_coord)
    J[2 * N : 3 * N, 0:N] = np.diag(y_coord)

    # dz/dy block: diag(x)
    J[2 * N : 3 * N, N : 2 * N] = np.diag(x)

    # dz/dz block: -beta * I
    J[2 * N : 3 * N, 2 * N : 3 * N] = -beta * np.eye(N)

    return J

def load_network(name: str = "16nodes") -> np.ndarray:
    """Load one of the example networks that ship with the package.

    Two undirected, unweighted, connected networks are included:

    - "16nodes": 16 nodes, 26 links; the network of the 16-node examples in
      Yildirim & Antonopoulos (2024).
    - "12nodes": 12 nodes, 14 links; the network of the 12-node examples
      (file `12nodes.txt` of the thesis code).

    Parameters
    ----------
    name : str, optional
        Name of the network, with or without the file extension
        ("16nodes" or "16nodes.txt"). Default is "16nodes".

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Adjacency matrix of floats, shape (M, M): 1 where two nodes are
        linked, 0 elsewhere; symmetric, with a zero diagonal.

    Raises
    ------
    FileNotFoundError
        If there is no network with this name. The message lists the
        available ones.
    """
    filename = name if name.endswith((".txt", ".csv")) else f"{name}.txt"
    file_ref = _DATA.joinpath(filename)

    if not file_ref.is_file():
        available = sorted(f.name.rsplit(".", 1)[0] for f in _DATA.iterdir() if f.name.endswith((".txt", ".csv")))
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"No network named '{name}' in the package. Available: {', '.join(available)}.")

    with file_ref.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return np.loadtxt(f, delimiter="\t")

docs.text: One-dimensional chaotic maps and networks of coupled maps.

docs.title: Local maps
docs.text:
Logistic map

\[ f(x) = r\,x\,(1 - x), \qquad f'(x) = r\,(1 - 2x) \]

Circle map

\[ f(x) = x + r - \frac{K}{2\pi}\sin(2\pi x) \pmod 1, \qquad f'(x) = 1 - K\cos(2\pi x) \]

Composite logistic map: the logistic map applied \(n\) times, \(f^n = f \circ \dots \circ f\), with derivative \(\prod_{k=0}^{n-1} f'(f^k(x))\). The thesis uses \(n = 3\).

docs.title: Coupled map network
docs.text:
simulate_discrete_models couples \(M\) maps on a network with adjacency matrix \(A\). With \(k_i\) the degree of node \(i\) and coupling strength \(\alpha\):

\[ x_i(n+1) = (1-\alpha)\, f\big(x_i(n)\big) + \frac{\alpha}{k_i}\sum_{j} A_{ij}\, f\big(x_j(n)\big) \]

A node with no links evolves as \((1-\alpha) f(x_i)\). The full Lyapunov spectrum comes from the Jacobian \(J = \big[(1-\alpha) I + \alpha W\big]\,\mathrm{diag}\big(f'(x)\big)\) with QR re-orthonormalization at every step.

import numpy as np
from complex_network_dynamics import load_network, logistic, df_logistic, simulate_discrete_models

A = load_network("16nodes")
x0 = np.random.rand(A.shape[0])

traj, lyap = simulate_discrete_models(x0, logistic, df_logistic, A, t=10_000, alpha=0.1, r=4.0)
traj.shape   # (10000, 16)
lyap[:3]     # largest Lyapunov exponents

Extra keyword arguments (here r=4.0) go to both f and df.

def logistic(x0, r=4):
    """Logistic map.

        f(x) = r x (1 - x)

    This is Eq. (14) of Yildirim & Antonopoulos (2024).

    Parameters
    ----------
    x0 : float or array_like
        Current state(s), usually in [0, 1].
    r : float, optional
        Growth parameter. r = 4 gives fully developed chaos. Default is 4.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Next state(s), with the same shape as `x0`.

    See Also
    --------
    df_logistic : Its derivative.
    """
    x0 = np.asarray(x0)
    y = r*x0*(1-x0)
    return y

def circle(x0, r=0.35, K=6.9115):
    """Circle map.

        f(x) = x + r - (K / 2 pi) sin(2 pi x)  (mod 1)

    This is Eq. (15) of Yildirim & Antonopoulos (2024) and Eq. (3.12) of the
    thesis; the defaults give chaotic dynamics (the paper rounds K to 6.91).

    Parameters
    ----------
    x0 : float or array_like
        Current state(s) in [0, 1).
    r : float, optional
        Rotation parameter. Default is 0.35.
    K : float, optional
        Nonlinearity strength. Default is 6.9115.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Next state(s) in [0, 1), with the same shape as `x0`.

    See Also
    --------
    df_circle : Its derivative.
    """
    x0 = np.asarray(x0)
    y = x0+r-(K/(2*math.pi))*np.sin(2*math.pi*x0)
    y = y%1
    return y

def df_circle(x, r=0.35, K=6.9115):

def composite_logistic(x0, r=4.0, n=3):
    """Logistic map applied n times.

        f^n(x) = f(f(...f(x)))

    Parameters
    ----------
    x0 : float or array_like
        Current state(s), usually in [0, 1].
    r : float, optional
        Growth parameter. Default is 4.0.
    n : int, optional
        Number of compositions. Default is 3, the order used in the thesis.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Next state(s), with the same shape as `x0`.

    See Also
    --------
    df_composite_logistic : Its derivative.
    """
    x = np.asarray(x0, dtype=float)
    for _ in range(n):
        x = r * x * (1 - x)
    return x

def df_composite_logistic(x, r=4.0, n=3):
    """Derivative of `composite_logistic`, by the chain rule.

        (f^n)'(x) = prod_{k=0}^{n-1} f'(f^k(x)),  with f'(x) = r (1 - 2x)

    Parameters
    ----------
    x : float or array_like
        State(s) at which to evaluate the derivative.
    r : float, optional
        Growth parameter. Default is 4.0.
    n : int, optional
        Number of compositions. Default is 3.

    Returns
    -------
    float or np.ndarray
        Derivative, with the same shape as `x`.
    """
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    product = np.ones_like(x)
    for _ in range(n):
        product = product * r * (1 - 2 * x)
        x = r * x * (1 - x)
    return product

Iterate coupled maps on a network and compute their Lyapunov spectrum.

Each node follows

x_i(n+1) = (1 - alpha) f(x_i(n)) + (alpha / k_i) sum_j A_ij f(x_j(n))

which is Eq. (13) of Yildirim & Antonopoulos (2024). Here k_i is the sum of row i of A (the in-degree for a directed network), and A[i, j] is the link from node j to node i. An isolated node (k_i = 0) evolves as (1 - alpha) f(x_i). The paper uses alpha = 0.1 for logistic maps and alpha = 0.03 for circle maps.

The spectrum is computed by evolving an orthonormal frame with the Jacobian (1 - alpha) I + alpha D^{-1} A, scaled column-wise by f'(x), and re-orthonormalising it by QR decomposition at every step.

Parameters:

required f callable

required df callable

required A array_like

Adjacency matrix, shape (M, M).

required t int

Number of recorded steps, including the first state after the transient. This is a number of iterations, not a time.

required alpha float

Coupling strength in [0, 1]. Default is 0.1.

0.1 n_transient int

Iterations discarded before recording, so the orbit reaches the attractor. Default is 1000.

1000 **params

Extra parameters passed to f and df, e.g. r=4.

{}

Name Type Description traj ndarray

Node states, shape (t, M).

lyap_exp ndarray

The M Lyapunov exponents, largest first.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If A is not square or x0 does not have M entries.

Notes

An orbit that lands exactly on a point where f' = 0 (for the logistic map with r = 4, x = 0.5, which then goes to 1 and 0) gives exponents of -inf with a "divide by zero" warning. This is correct for that orbit; start from random states to avoid it.

def simulate_discrete_models(x0, f, df, A, t, alpha=0.1, n_transient=1000, **params):
    """Iterate coupled maps on a network and compute their Lyapunov spectrum.

    Each node follows

        x_i(n+1) = (1 - alpha) f(x_i(n)) + (alpha / k_i) sum_j A_ij f(x_j(n))

    which is Eq. (13) of Yildirim & Antonopoulos (2024). Here k_i is the sum
    of row i of A (the in-degree for a directed network), and A[i, j] is the
    link from node j to node i. An isolated node (k_i = 0) evolves as
    (1 - alpha) f(x_i). The paper uses alpha = 0.1 for logistic maps and
    alpha = 0.03 for circle maps.

    The spectrum is computed by evolving an orthonormal frame with the
    Jacobian (1 - alpha) I + alpha D^{-1} A, scaled column-wise by f'(x),
    and re-orthonormalising it by QR decomposition at every step.

    Parameters
    ----------
    x0 : array_like
        Initial states of the M nodes, shape (M,).
    f : callable
        Map of one node, f(x, **params), e.g. `logistic` or `circle`.
    df : callable
        Its derivative, df(x, **params), e.g. `df_logistic` or `df_circle`.
    A : array_like
        Adjacency matrix, shape (M, M).
    t : int
        Number of recorded steps, including the first state after the
        transient. This is a number of iterations, not a time.
    alpha : float, optional
        Coupling strength in [0, 1]. Default is 0.1.
    n_transient : int, optional
        Iterations discarded before recording, so the orbit reaches the
        attractor. Default is 1000.
    **params
        Extra parameters passed to `f` and `df`, e.g. r=4.

    Returns
    -------
    traj : np.ndarray
        Node states, shape (t, M).
    lyap_exp : np.ndarray
        The M Lyapunov exponents, largest first.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `A` is not square or `x0` does not have M entries.

    Notes
    -----
    An orbit that lands exactly on a point where f' = 0 (for the logistic map
    with r = 4, x = 0.5, which then goes to 1 and 0) gives exponents of -inf
    with a "divide by zero" warning. This is correct for that orbit; start
    from random states to avoid it.
    """
    x = np.asarray(x0, dtype=float).ravel().copy()
    A = np.asarray(A, dtype=float)
    M = A.shape[0]
    if A.shape != (M, M) or x.size != M:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Dimension mismatch: A of shape {A.shape} expects {M} initial states, but got x0 of size {x.size}"
        )

    # Precompute row-normalized transition matrix W
    degree = np.sum(A, axis=1)
    degree_safe = np.where(degree == 0, 1.0, degree)
    W = A / degree_safe[:, np.newaxis]

    # Isolated nodes keep a zero row in W, so they evolve as (1 - alpha) * f(x_i)

    # Effective linear coupling operator: M_net = (1 - alpha) * I + alpha * W
    M_net = (1.0 - alpha) * np.eye(M) + alpha * W

    # 1. Transient burn-in (lets state settle onto the attractor)
    for _ in range(n_transient):
        f_x = f(x, **params)
        x = M_net @ f_x

    # 2. Main loop: recording trajectories and tracking perturbations
    traj = np.zeros((t, M), dtype=float)
    traj[0] = x

    # Initialize orthonormal tangent frame Q and running sum of log expansion rates
    Q = np.eye(M, dtype=float)
    lyap_sum = np.zeros(M, dtype=float)

    for step in range(1, t):
        # Local state and local derivatives
        f_x = f(x, **params)
        f_prime = df(x, **params)  # shape: (M,)

        # Next state
        x = M_net @ f_x
        traj[step] = x

        # Jacobian J = M_net @ diag(f')
        # Efficient column-scaling: M_net * f_prime avoids an explicit diag() allocation
        J = M_net * f_prime

        # Propagate tangent vectors: Z = J @ Q
        Z = J @ Q

        # Re-orthonormalize via QR decomposition
        Q, R = np.linalg.qr(Z)

        # Accumulate log expansion factors (diagonal elements of upper-triangular R)
        # abs avoids negative values from possible reflection components
        lyap_sum += np.log(np.abs(np.diag(R)))

    # Compute average rates of divergence
    lyap_exp = lyap_sum / (t - 1)
    lyap_exp = np.sort(lyap_exp)[::-1]  # Sort descending (lambda_1 >= lambda_2 >= ...)

    return traj, lyap_exp

docs.title: Integrators
docs.text:
Integrate a system and compute its Lyapunov spectrum at the same time.

Alongside the state \(y\), each integrator evolves an orthonormal tangent frame \(Q\) with the variational equation \(\dot Q = J(t, y)\,Q\). Every few steps \(Q\) is re-orthonormalized by a QR decomposition \(Q = Q' R\), and the Lyapunov exponents are the time-averaged logarithms of the diagonal of \(R\):

\[ \lambda_i = \lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{T} \sum_k \ln |R^{(k)}_{ii}| \]

docs.title: Which integrator?
docs.text: Function Method Speed Needs euler_with_lyapunov Forward Euler, fixed step fast, low accuracy NumPy model rk4_with_lyapunov RK4, fixed step good default NumPy model solve_ivp_with_lyapunov SciPy adaptive (RK45, DOP853, …) slower, most accurate NumPy model build_rk4_lyapunov RK4, compiled with Numba; same results as rk4_with_lyapunov about 10× faster Numba (*_njit) model

docs.title: Shared names
docs.text:
All integrators use the same names: f, df (vector field and Jacobian), y0, t0 (initial state and time), h (step size), n_steps (recorded points), n_transient (steps discarded first), qr_interval (steps between QR re-orthonormalisations) and lyap_mode. solve_ivp_with_lyapunov is adaptive, so it takes the recorded time t_total and the window length dt_qr instead of h, n_steps and qr_interval, and counts n_transient in windows of dt_qr.

Time runs on through the transient: the first recorded point is at t0 + n_transient * h (t0 + n_transient * dt_qr for solve_ivp_with_lyapunov).

docs.title: The lyap_mode option
docs.text:
All integrators accept lyap_mode:

lyap_mode Returns "none" t_vals, traj "spectrum" (default) t_vals, traj, spectrum "history" t_vals, traj, lyap_times, lyap_history

Use "history" to check that the exponents have converged.

def euler_with_lyapunov(
    f,
    y0,
    t0,
    h,
    n_steps,
    df=None,
    lyap_mode="spectrum",
    n_transient=1000,
    qr_interval=10,
    **params,
):
    """Integrate dy/dt = f(t, y) by forward Euler, with the Lyapunov spectrum.

    The tangent frame is evolved alongside the state, Q -> (I + h J) Q, and
    re-orthonormalised by QR decomposition every `qr_interval` steps.

    Parameters
    ----------
    f : callable
        Vector field f(t, y, **params).
    y0 : array_like
        Initial state.
    t0 : float
        Initial time.
    h : float
        Fixed step size.
    n_steps : int
        Number of recorded points after the transient (n_steps - 1 steps).
    df : callable, optional
        Jacobian df(t, y, **params). Required unless lyap_mode="none".
    lyap_mode : {"none", "spectrum", "history"}, optional
        What to compute besides the trajectory. Default is "spectrum".
    n_transient : int, optional
        Steps discarded before recording. Default is 1000.
    qr_interval : int, optional
        Number of steps between QR re-orthonormalisations. Default is 10.
    **params
        Extra keyword arguments passed to `f` and `df`.

    Returns
    -------
    t_vals : np.ndarray
        Times, shape (n_steps,), starting at t0 + n_transient * h.
    traj : np.ndarray
        Trajectory, shape (n_steps, d).
    spectrum : np.ndarray
        Only if lyap_mode="spectrum": Lyapunov exponents, largest first, shape (d,).
    lyap_times, lyap_history : np.ndarray
        Only if lyap_mode="history": the time of each QR step and the running
        Lyapunov estimates at those times, shape (n_qr, d).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `lyap_mode` is invalid, `df` is missing, or `n_steps` is too small
        for `qr_interval`.

    See Also
    --------
    rk4_with_lyapunov : Fourth-order Runge-Kutta, far more accurate for the same step.
    """
    n_qr = _check_options(lyap_mode, df, n_steps, qr_interval)

    y = np.asarray(y0, dtype=float).ravel().copy()
    d = len(y)
    t = float(t0)

    def eval_f(t_eval, y_eval):
        return np.asarray(f(t_eval, y_eval, **params), dtype=float).ravel()

    # Transient (state only)
    for _ in range(n_transient):
        y += h * eval_f(t, y)
        t += h

    traj = np.zeros((n_steps, d), dtype=float)
    t_vals = np.zeros(n_steps, dtype=float)
    traj[0] = y
    t_vals[0] = t

    if lyap_mode == "none":
        for step in range(1, n_steps):
            y += h * eval_f(t, y)
            t += h
            traj[step] = y
            t_vals[step] = t
        return t_vals, traj

    Q = np.eye(d, dtype=float)
    lyap_sum = np.zeros(d, dtype=float)
    lyap_times = np.zeros(n_qr, dtype=float)
    lyap_history = np.zeros((n_qr, d), dtype=float)
    qr_idx = 0

    for step in range(1, n_steps):
        fn = eval_f(t, y)
        Jn = np.asarray(df(t, y, **params), dtype=float)

        y += h * fn
        t += h
        traj[step] = y
        t_vals[step] = t

        # Variational step: Q_next = (I + h J) Q
        Q += h * (Jn @ Q)

        if step % qr_interval == 0:
            Q = _qr_step(Q, lyap_sum)
            if lyap_mode == "history":
                lyap_history[qr_idx] = lyap_sum / (step * h)
                lyap_times[qr_idx] = t
                qr_idx += 1

    return _results(lyap_mode, t_vals, traj, lyap_sum, n_qr * qr_interval * h, lyap_times, lyap_history)

def rk4_with_lyapunov(
    f,
    y0,
    t0,
    h,
    n_steps,
    df=None,
    lyap_mode="spectrum",
    n_transient=1000,
    qr_interval=10,
    **params,
):
    """Integrate dy/dt = f(t, y) by fourth-order Runge-Kutta, with the Lyapunov spectrum.

    The state and the tangent frame are advanced together by RK4, and the
    frame is re-orthonormalised by QR decomposition every `qr_interval` steps.

    Parameters
    ----------
    f : callable
        Vector field f(t, y, **params).
    y0 : array_like
        Initial state.
    t0 : float
        Initial time.
    h : float
        Fixed step size.
    n_steps : int
        Number of recorded points after the transient (n_steps - 1 steps).
    df : callable, optional
        Jacobian df(t, y, **params). Required unless lyap_mode="none".
    lyap_mode : {"none", "spectrum", "history"}, optional
        What to compute besides the trajectory. Default is "spectrum".
    n_transient : int, optional
        Steps discarded before recording. Default is 1000.
    qr_interval : int, optional
        Number of steps between QR re-orthonormalisations. Default is 10.
    **params
        Extra keyword arguments passed to `f` and `df`.

    Returns
    -------
    t_vals : np.ndarray
        Times, shape (n_steps,), starting at t0 + n_transient * h.
    traj : np.ndarray
        Trajectory, shape (n_steps, d).
    spectrum : np.ndarray
        Only if lyap_mode="spectrum": Lyapunov exponents, largest first, shape (d,).
    lyap_times, lyap_history : np.ndarray
        Only if lyap_mode="history": the time of each QR step and the running
        Lyapunov estimates at those times, shape (n_qr, d).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `lyap_mode` is invalid, `df` is missing, or `n_steps` is too small
        for `qr_interval`.

    See Also
    --------
    build_rk4_lyapunov : The same method compiled with Numba, about 10 times faster.
    """
    n_qr = _check_options(lyap_mode, df, n_steps, qr_interval)

    y = np.asarray(y0, dtype=float).ravel().copy()
    d = len(y)
    t = float(t0)

    def eval_f(t_eval, y_eval):
        return np.asarray(f(t_eval, y_eval, **params), dtype=float).ravel()

    def rk4_state_step(t, y):
        k1 = eval_f(t, y)
        k2 = eval_f(t + 0.5 * h, y + 0.5 * h * k1)
        k3 = eval_f(t + 0.5 * h, y + 0.5 * h * k2)
        k4 = eval_f(t + h, y + h * k3)
        return y + (h / 6.0) * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4)

    # Transient (state only)
    for _ in range(n_transient):
        y = rk4_state_step(t, y)
        t += h

    traj = np.zeros((n_steps, d), dtype=float)
    t_vals = np.zeros(n_steps, dtype=float)
    traj[0] = y
    t_vals[0] = t

    if lyap_mode == "none":
        for step in range(1, n_steps):
            y = rk4_state_step(t, y)
            t += h
            traj[step] = y
            t_vals[step] = t
        return t_vals, traj

    Q = np.eye(d, dtype=float)
    lyap_sum = np.zeros(d, dtype=float)
    lyap_times = np.zeros(n_qr, dtype=float)
    lyap_history = np.zeros((n_qr, d), dtype=float)
    qr_idx = 0

    for step in range(1, n_steps):
        # Stage 1
        k1 = eval_f(t, y)
        J1 = np.asarray(df(t, y, **params), dtype=float)
        K1_Q = J1 @ Q

        # Stage 2
        y2 = y + 0.5 * h * k1
        t2 = t + 0.5 * h
        k2 = eval_f(t2, y2)
        J2 = np.asarray(df(t2, y2, **params), dtype=float)
        K2_Q = J2 @ (Q + 0.5 * h * K1_Q)

        # Stage 3
        y3 = y + 0.5 * h * k2
        k3 = eval_f(t2, y3)
        J3 = np.asarray(df(t2, y3, **params), dtype=float)
        K3_Q = J3 @ (Q + 0.5 * h * K2_Q)

        # Stage 4
        y4 = y + h * k3
        t4 = t + h
        k4 = eval_f(t4, y4)
        J4 = np.asarray(df(t4, y4, **params), dtype=float)
        K4_Q = J4 @ (Q + h * K3_Q)

        y = y + (h / 6.0) * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4)
        Q = Q + (h / 6.0) * (K1_Q + 2 * K2_Q + 2 * K3_Q + K4_Q)
        t += h
        traj[step] = y
        t_vals[step] = t

        if step % qr_interval == 0:
            Q = _qr_step(Q, lyap_sum)
            if lyap_mode == "history":
                lyap_history[qr_idx] = lyap_sum / (step * h)
                lyap_times[qr_idx] = t
                qr_idx += 1

    return _results(lyap_mode, t_vals, traj, lyap_sum, n_qr * qr_interval * h, lyap_times, lyap_history)

def solve_ivp_with_lyapunov(
    f,
    y0,
    t0,
    t_total,
    df=None,
    lyap_mode="spectrum",
    n_transient=200,
    dt_qr=0.05,
    method="RK45",
    rtol=1e-7,
    atol=1e-9,
    **params,
):
    """Integrate dy/dt = f(t, y) by an adaptive SciPy solver, with the Lyapunov spectrum.

    The state and the tangent frame are integrated together by
    `scipy.integrate.solve_ivp` over windows of length `dt_qr`; after each
    window the frame is re-orthonormalised by QR decomposition and the state
    is recorded.

    Parameters
    ----------
    f : callable
        Vector field f(t, y, **params).
    y0 : array_like
        Initial state.
    t0 : float
        Initial time.
    t_total : float
        Integration time recorded after the transient.
    df : callable, optional
        Jacobian df(t, y, **params). Required unless lyap_mode="none".
    lyap_mode : {"none", "spectrum", "history"}, optional
        What to compute besides the trajectory. Default is "spectrum".
    n_transient : int, optional
        Windows of length `dt_qr` discarded before recording. Default is 200.
    dt_qr : float, optional
        Length of each window: the time between QR re-orthonormalisations
        and between recorded points. Default is 0.05.
    method : str, optional
        Any `scipy.integrate.solve_ivp` method. Default is "RK45".
    rtol, atol : float, optional
        Solver tolerances. Defaults are 1e-7 and 1e-9.
    **params
        Extra keyword arguments passed to `f` and `df` (e.g. A, K, sigma).

    Returns
    -------
    t_vals : np.ndarray
        Times, shape (n_windows + 1,), starting at t0 + n_transient * dt_qr,
        where n_windows = round(t_total / dt_qr).
    traj : np.ndarray
        Trajectory sampled every `dt_qr`, shape (n_windows + 1, d).
    spectrum : np.ndarray
        Only if lyap_mode="spectrum": Lyapunov exponents, largest first, shape (d,).
    lyap_times, lyap_history : np.ndarray
        Only if lyap_mode="history": the time of each QR step and the running
        Lyapunov estimates at those times, shape (n_windows, d).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `lyap_mode` is invalid or `df` is missing.

    See Also
    --------
    rk4_with_lyapunov : Fixed-step RK4, faster for smooth systems.
    """
    _check_options(lyap_mode, df, 2, 1)

    y = np.asarray(y0, dtype=float).ravel().copy()
    d = len(y)
    t = float(t0)

    def f_eval(t_eval, y_eval):
        return np.asarray(f(t_eval, y_eval, **params), dtype=float).ravel()

    def augmented_rhs(t_eval, y_aug):
        state = y_aug[:d]
        Q_mat = y_aug[d:].reshape(d, d)
        J = np.asarray(df(t_eval, state, **params), dtype=float)
        return np.concatenate([f_eval(t_eval, state), (J @ Q_mat).ravel()])

    # Transient (state only)
    t_transient = n_transient * dt_qr
    if t_transient > 0:
        sol = solve_ivp(f_eval, (t, t + t_transient), y, method=method, rtol=rtol, atol=atol)
        y = sol.y[:, -1]
        t = sol.t[-1]

    n_windows = max(1, int(round(t_total / dt_qr)))
    traj = np.zeros((n_windows + 1, d), dtype=float)
    t_vals = np.zeros(n_windows + 1, dtype=float)
    traj[0] = y
    t_vals[0] = t
    t_start = t

    Q = np.eye(d, dtype=float)
    lyap_sum = np.zeros(d, dtype=float)
    lyap_times = np.zeros(n_windows, dtype=float)
    lyap_history = np.zeros((n_windows, d), dtype=float)

    for step in range(n_windows):
        t_end = t_start + (step + 1) * dt_qr
        if lyap_mode == "none":
            sol = solve_ivp(f_eval, (t, t_end), y, method=method, rtol=rtol, atol=atol)
            y = sol.y[:, -1]
        else:
            sol = solve_ivp(augmented_rhs, (t, t_end), np.concatenate([y, Q.ravel()]),
                            method=method, rtol=rtol, atol=atol)
            y = sol.y[:d, -1]
            Q = _qr_step(sol.y[d:, -1].reshape(d, d), lyap_sum)
            lyap_history[step] = lyap_sum / (t_end - t_start)
            lyap_times[step] = t_end
        t = t_end
        traj[step + 1] = y
        t_vals[step + 1] = t

    return _results(lyap_mode, t_vals, traj, lyap_sum, n_windows * dt_qr, lyap_times, lyap_history)

f and df are compiled into the solver, so it runs entirely in machine code, about 10 times faster than rk4_with_lyapunov. The solver uses the same method, names and outputs as rk4_with_lyapunov and gives the same results, except that the model parameters are passed as a tuple args.

The first call compiles the solver, which takes a few seconds.

def build_rk4_lyapunov(f, df):
    """Build a Numba-compiled `rk4_with_lyapunov` for one system.

    `f` and `df` are compiled into the solver, so it runs entirely in machine
    code, about 10 times faster than `rk4_with_lyapunov`. The solver uses the
    same method, names and outputs as `rk4_with_lyapunov` and gives the same
    results, except that the model parameters are passed as a tuple `args`.

    Parameters
    ----------
    f : callable
        Numba-compiled vector field f(t, y, args), e.g. `lorenz_njit`.
    df : callable
        Numba-compiled Jacobian df(t, y, args), e.g. `lorenz_jacobian_njit`.

    Returns
    -------
    callable
        solver(y0, t0, h, n_steps, args, lyap_mode="spectrum", n_transient=1000,
        qr_interval=10), returning (t_vals, traj) for lyap_mode="none",
        (t_vals, traj, spectrum) for "spectrum" and
        (t_vals, traj, lyap_times, lyap_history) for "history", exactly as
        `rk4_with_lyapunov`. The first call compiles the solver, which takes
        a few seconds.

    See Also
    --------
    rk4_with_lyapunov : The same method in plain Python, with keyword parameters.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> solver = build_rk4_lyapunov(lorenz_njit, lorenz_jacobian_njit)
    >>> t, traj, spectrum = solver(np.ones(3), 0.0, 0.01, 50_000, (10.0, 28.0, 8 / 3))
    """

    @njit
    def rk4_core(y0, t0, h, n_steps, args, compute_lyap, n_transient, qr_interval):
        d = len(y0)
        y = np.copy(y0)
        t = t0

        # Transient (state only)
        for _ in range(n_transient):
            k1 = f(t, y, args)
            k2 = f(t + 0.5 * h, y + 0.5 * h * k1, args)
            k3 = f(t + 0.5 * h, y + 0.5 * h * k2, args)
            k4 = f(t + h, y + h * k3, args)
            y = y + (h / 6.0) * (k1 + 2.0 * k2 + 2.0 * k3 + k4)
            t += h

        traj = np.zeros((n_steps, d), dtype=np.float64)
        t_vals = np.zeros(n_steps, dtype=np.float64)
        traj[0] = y
        t_vals[0] = t

        n_qr = (n_steps - 1) // qr_interval if compute_lyap else 0
        Q = np.eye(d, dtype=np.float64)
        lyap_sum = np.zeros(d, dtype=np.float64)
        lyap_times = np.zeros(n_qr, dtype=np.float64)
        lyap_history = np.zeros((n_qr, d), dtype=np.float64)
        qr_idx = 0

        for step in range(1, n_steps):
            k1 = f(t, y, args)
            y2 = y + 0.5 * h * k1
            t2 = t + 0.5 * h
            k2 = f(t2, y2, args)
            y3 = y + 0.5 * h * k2
            k3 = f(t2, y3, args)
            y4 = y + h * k3
            t4 = t + h
            k4 = f(t4, y4, args)

            if compute_lyap:
                K1_Q = df(t, y, args) @ Q
                K2_Q = df(t2, y2, args) @ (Q + 0.5 * h * K1_Q)
                K3_Q = df(t2, y3, args) @ (Q + 0.5 * h * K2_Q)
                K4_Q = df(t4, y4, args) @ (Q + h * K3_Q)
                Q = Q + (h / 6.0) * (K1_Q + 2.0 * K2_Q + 2.0 * K3_Q + K4_Q)

            y = y + (h / 6.0) * (k1 + 2.0 * k2 + 2.0 * k3 + k4)
            t += h
            traj[step] = y
            t_vals[step] = t

            if compute_lyap and step % qr_interval == 0:
                Q, lyap_sum = _apply_qr_update(Q, lyap_sum)
                lyap_history[qr_idx, :] = lyap_sum / (step * h)
                lyap_times[qr_idx] = t
                qr_idx += 1

        return t_vals, traj, lyap_sum, lyap_times, lyap_history

    def solver(y0, t0, h, n_steps, args, lyap_mode="spectrum", n_transient=1000, qr_interval=10):
        n_qr = _check_options(lyap_mode, df, n_steps, qr_interval)
        t_vals, traj, lyap_sum, lyap_times, lyap_history = rk4_core(
            np.asarray(y0, dtype=np.float64).ravel().copy(), float(t0), float(h), int(n_steps), args,
            lyap_mode != "none", int(n_transient), int(qr_interval),
        )
        return _results(lyap_mode, t_vals, traj, lyap_sum, n_qr * qr_interval * h, lyap_times, lyap_history)

    return solver

docs.title: Network Inference
docs.text: Reconstruct a network from the time series of its nodes using the Mutual Information Rate (MIR).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
For every pair of nodes \((i, j)\):

  1. The joint trajectory \((x_i, x_j)\) is normalized and binned on an \(N \times N\) grid.
  2. The mutual information \(I_{ij}\) is computed from the grid occupancy: [ I_{ij} = \sum_{a,b} p_{ab} \ln \frac{p_{ab}}{p_a\, p_b} ]
  3. The correlation decay time \(T_{ij}\) is the largest shortest path in the graph of cell-to-cell transitions (corr_decay).
  4. MIR is \(I_{ij} / T_{ij}\), averaged over a range of grid sizes \(N\) chosen by Grid.

Pairs with high MIR are likely to be directly connected.

docs.title: Deciding which links are real: surrogate test
docs.text:
A high MIR alone does not say where to draw the line between links and non-links. mir_surrogate_test compares the MIR of each pair with its MIR on \(1/p_{sl}\) surrogate datasets:

  1. The p-value of a pair is the fraction of surrogates whose MIR is at least the MIR of the data.
  2. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (fdr_bh) controls the false discovery rate, with \(q = p_{sl}/100\) by default, as in the thesis code.
  3. If the true network is known, tpr_fpr gives the true and false positive rates.

The test can be repeated for growing data lengths (time_range) to see how much data the inference needs.

docs.title: More MIR tools
docs.text:
Function What it does double_normalised_mir MIR min-max scaled per grid size, summed over grid sizes and scaled to a maximum of 1; with the true network, the best reconstruction rate over thresholds lagged_double_mir As above, but each pair uses its largest MI over time lags \(-L,\dots,L\), for links with a delay best_case_tpr_fpr ROC sweep over all thresholds of a similarity matrix, and the threshold closest to perfect inference 
from complex_network_dynamics import double_normalised_mir, best_case_tpr_fpr, load_network

A = load_network("16nodes")
normalised, max_rate = double_normalised_mir(traj, true_network=A)
roc, best, inferred = best_case_tpr_fpr(normalised, A)
best   # TPR, FPR, distance to (0, 1), threshold

Grid sizes

lagged_double_mir uses a slightly different grid-size rule from Grid: its search continues while the average points per cell equals the number of occupied cells, and the largest grid size is not capped at 30.

plot_similarity_gap_bars compares the MIR values with the true network and shows whether a threshold can separate true edges from non-edges.

import numpy as np
from complex_network_dynamics import (
    load_network, logistic, df_logistic, simulate_discrete_models, MIR, plot_similarity_gap_bars,
)

A = load_network("16nodes")
traj, _ = simulate_discrete_models(np.random.rand(16), logistic, df_logistic, A, t=10_000, alpha=0.1)

Mutual Information Rate (MIR) between every pair of nodes.

For each grid size N in the partition range, MIR is the mutual information divided by the correlation decay time (corr_decay). Results are averaged over all grid sizes. Higher MIR suggests a direct link.

Parameters:

required N_range tuple of int

(N_min, N_max) grid sizes. If None, chosen automatically by Grid.

None nodes tuple of int

def MIR(Dat, N_range=None, nodes=None):
  """Mutual Information Rate (MIR) between every pair of nodes.

  For each grid size N in the partition range, MIR is the mutual information
  divided by the correlation decay time (`corr_decay`). Results are averaged
  over all grid sizes. Higher MIR suggests a direct link.

  Parameters
  ----------
  Dat : array_like
      Time series, shape (npts, M): one column per node.
  N_range : tuple of int, optional
      (N_min, N_max) grid sizes. If None, chosen automatically by `Grid`.
  nodes : tuple of int, optional
      (i, j) with i <= j. If given, plots how MI and MIR for this pair
      change with the grid size.

  Returns
  -------
  Mir : np.ndarray
      MIR matrix, shape (M, M).
  Mi : np.ndarray
      Mutual information matrix, shape (M, M).
  """
  Dat = np.ascontiguousarray(Dat, dtype=np.float64)
  M = Dat.shape[1]
  pi, pj = np.triu_indices(M)  # pairs with i <= j, diagonal included

  if N_range is None:
    N_min, N_max = Grid(Dat)
  else:
    N_min, N_max = int(N_range[0]), int(N_range[1])

  partition_range = np.arange(N_min, N_max + 1)
  num_partitions = len(partition_range)

  Is = np.zeros((M, M))
  Ic = np.zeros((M, M))
  Mi_MIR_over_partitions = np.zeros((2, num_partitions))

  for idx, N in enumerate(partition_range):
    I_s = np.zeros((M, M))
    I_c = np.zeros((M, M))

    mi, t = _pairs_mi_and_decay(Dat, pi, pj, int(N))
    I_s[pi, pj] = mi
    I_s[pj, pi] = mi
    I_c[pi, pj] = mi / t
    I_c[pj, pi] = mi / t

    if nodes is not None:
      Mi_MIR_over_partitions[0, idx] = I_s[nodes[0], nodes[1]]
      Mi_MIR_over_partitions[1, idx] = I_c[nodes[0], nodes[1]]

    Is += I_s
    Ic += I_c

  Mir = Ic / num_partitions
  Mi = Is / num_partitions

  if nodes is not None:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))

    # MI plot (linear x, log y)
    axes[0].semilogy(partition_range, Mi_MIR_over_partitions[0, :], "o--")
    axes[0].set_title(f"Evolution of MI for nodes {nodes} over partitions")
    axes[0].set_xlabel("Partition Size N")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("MI")
    axes[0].grid(True, which="both", ls="--")

    # MIR plot (linear x, log y)
    axes[1].semilogy(partition_range, Mi_MIR_over_partitions[1, :], ".-")
    axes[1].set_title(f"Evolution of MIR for nodes {nodes} over partitions")
    axes[1].set_xlabel("Partition Size N")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("MIR")
    axes[1].grid(True, which="both", ls="--")

    # Enforce integer ticks on x-axis for both subplots
    for ax in axes:
      if len(partition_range) <= 15:
        ax.set_xticks(partition_range)
      else:
        ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(MaxNLocator(integer=True))

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

  return Mir, Mi

Infer a network with MIR and a surrogate data test.

For each data length in time_range, MIR is computed for every pair of nodes in the data and in 1/p_sl surrogate datasets. A pair's p-value is the fraction of surrogates whose MIR is at least the MIR of the data. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (fdr_bh) then decides which pairs are linked. This is the method of Yildirim & Antonopoulos (2024) and of the thesis code Mir_surrogate_data.m; the paper uses p_sl = 0.1 (10 surrogates) on the 11 x 11 grid of pc_amplitude, pc_phase = 0, 0.1, ..., 1.

def mir_surrogate_test(data, p_sl=0.01, time_range=None, surrogate="amplitude_phase", true_network=None,
                       pc_amplitude=1.0, pc_phase=0.5, fdr_q=None, rng=None):
  """Infer a network with MIR and a surrogate data test.

  For each data length in `time_range`, MIR is computed for every pair of
  nodes in the data and in 1/p_sl surrogate datasets. A pair's p-value is the
  fraction of surrogates whose MIR is at least the MIR of the data. The
  Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (`fdr_bh`) then decides which pairs are linked.
  This is the method of Yildirim & Antonopoulos (2024) and of the thesis
  code `Mir_surrogate_data.m`; the paper uses p_sl = 0.1 (10 surrogates) on
  the 11 x 11 grid of pc_amplitude, pc_phase = 0, 0.1, ..., 1.

  With the default false discovery rate q = p_sl / 100, the smallest nonzero
  p-value, 1/n_surrogates, never passes, so a pair is linked exactly when the
  MIR of the data exceeds the MIR of every surrogate.

  Parameters
  ----------
  data : array_like
      Time series after the transient, shape (n_points, n_nodes), with at
      least two nodes.
  p_sl : float, optional
      Significance level; also sets the number of surrogates, 1/p_sl.
      Default is 0.01 (100 surrogates).
  time_range : sequence of int, optional
      Data lengths to test, each using the first that many points.
      Default is the full length only.
  surrogate : str or callable, optional
      "amplitude_phase" (APMSD), "phaseran", "random" or
      "correlated_random", or a function f(data, rng) returning one surrogate of shape
      (n_points, n_nodes). Default is "amplitude_phase".
  true_network : array_like, optional
      Ground-truth adjacency matrix. If given, TPR and FPR are computed.
  pc_amplitude, pc_phase : float, optional
      Fractions of time points whose amplitudes and phases are randomised
      by the "amplitude_phase" surrogates. Defaults are 1 and 0.5.
  fdr_q : float, optional
      False discovery rate for `fdr_bh`. Default is p_sl / 100.
  rng : numpy.random.Generator or int, optional
      Random generator or seed for the surrogates.

  Returns
  -------
  mir_overall : np.ndarray
      Shape (len(time_range), 1 + n_surrogates, n_pairs). Row 0 holds the MIR
      of the data, the other rows the MIR of each surrogate. Pairs are in the
      order (0, 1), (0, 2), ..., (1, 2), ...
  adjacency : np.ndarray
      Inferred symmetric adjacency matrices after FDR, shape
      (len(time_range), n_nodes, n_nodes).
  tp_fp_rate : np.ndarray
      Shape (len(time_range), 3): data length, TPR and FPR (NaN without
      `true_network`).

  Raises
  ------
  ValueError
      If `data` is not an (n_points, n_nodes) array with at least two nodes,
      the surrogate type is unknown, or `true_network` is not binary.
  """
  data = np.asarray(data, dtype=float)
  if data.ndim != 2 or data.shape[1] < 2:
    raise ValueError(
      f"data must have shape (n_points, n_nodes) with at least two nodes, one column per node; "
      f"got shape {data.shape}. A single node has no links to infer."
    )
  n_points, n_nodes = data.shape
  if true_network is not None:
    tpr_fpr(true_network, true_network)  # check it is binary before the long computation
  rng = np.random.default_rng(rng)
  n_surrogates = int(round(1 / p_sl))
  fdr_q = p_sl / 100 if fdr_q is None else fdr_q
  time_range = [n_points] if time_range is None else [min(int(t), n_points) for t in time_range]

  if callable(surrogate):
    make_surrogate = lambda d: surrogate(d, rng)
  elif surrogate in _SURROGATE_GENERATORS:
    generator = _SURROGATE_GENERATORS[surrogate]
    make_surrogate = lambda d: generator(d, rng, pc_amplitude, pc_phase)
  else:
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown surrogate type '{surrogate}'.")

  pairs = np.triu_indices(n_nodes, k=1)
  n_pairs = len(pairs[0])
  mir_overall = np.zeros((len(time_range), 1 + n_surrogates, n_pairs))
  adjacency = np.zeros((len(time_range), n_nodes, n_nodes))
  tp_fp_rate = np.full((len(time_range), 3), np.nan)
  tp_fp_rate[:, 0] = time_range

  for it, length in enumerate(time_range):
    segment = data[:length]
    mir_overall[it, 0] = MIR(segment)[0][pairs]
    for k in range(n_surrogates):
      mir_overall[it, 1 + k] = MIR(make_surrogate(segment))[0][pairs]

    p_values = np.sum(mir_overall[it, 1:] >= mir_overall[it, 0], axis=0) / n_surrogates
    h, _, _, _ = fdr_bh(p_values, fdr_q, "pdep")
    adjacency[it][pairs] = h
    adjacency[it] += adjacency[it].T

    if true_network is not None:
      tp_fp_rate[it, 1:] = tpr_fpr(true_network, adjacency[it])

  return mir_overall, adjacency, tp_fp_rate

def fdr_bh(pvals, q=0.05, method="pdep"):
  """Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure.

  Parameters
  ----------
  pvals : array_like
      p-values, any shape.
  q : float, optional
      False discovery rate. Default is 0.05.
  method : {"pdep", "dep"}, optional
      "pdep" assumes independent or positively dependent tests
      (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995); "dep" allows any dependence
      (Benjamini & Yekutieli, 2001). Default is "pdep".

  Returns
  -------
  h : np.ndarray
      Boolean array, same shape as `pvals`: True where the null hypothesis
      is rejected.
  crit_p : float
      Largest p-value that is still significant (0 if none is).
  adj_ci_cvrg : float
      FDR-adjusted confidence interval coverage (NaN if nothing is significant).
  adj_p : np.ndarray
      FDR-adjusted p-values, same shape as `pvals`.
  """
  pvals = np.asarray(pvals, dtype=float)
  if np.any(pvals < 0):
    raise ValueError("Some p-values are less than 0.")
  if np.any(pvals > 1):
    raise ValueError("Some p-values are greater than 1.")

  flat = pvals.ravel()
  sort_ids = np.argsort(flat, kind="stable")
  p_sorted = flat[sort_ids]
  m = len(p_sorted)
  ranks = np.arange(1, m + 1)

  if method == "pdep":
    thresh = ranks * q / m
    wtd_p = m * p_sorted / ranks
  elif method == "dep":
    denom = m * np.sum(1.0 / ranks)
    thresh = ranks * q / denom
    wtd_p = denom * p_sorted / ranks
  else:
    raise ValueError("Argument 'method' needs to be 'pdep' or 'dep'.")

  # Adjusted p-values: each p gets the smallest weighted p at or after its rank
  adj_sorted = np.full(m, np.nan)
  wtd_sindex = np.argsort(wtd_p, kind="stable")
  nextfill = 0
  for k in range(m):
    if wtd_sindex[k] >= nextfill:
      adj_sorted[nextfill:wtd_sindex[k] + 1] = wtd_p[wtd_sindex[k]]
      nextfill = wtd_sindex[k] + 1
      if nextfill >= m:
        break
  adj_p = np.empty(m)
  adj_p[sort_ids] = adj_sorted

  rejected = np.nonzero(p_sorted <= thresh)[0]
  if len(rejected) == 0:
    return np.zeros(pvals.shape, dtype=bool), 0.0, np.nan, adj_p.reshape(pvals.shape)
  max_id = rejected[-1]
  crit_p = p_sorted[max_id]
  return pvals <= crit_p, crit_p, 1 - thresh[max_id], adj_p.reshape(pvals.shape)

tpr_fpr(true_adjacency, inferred_adjacency)

True and false positive rates of an inferred network.

The two matrices are compared entry by entry over the whole M x M matrix, as in the thesis code (TPR_FPR.m): each link of a symmetric network is counted twice, and the diagonal, which is 0 in both, adds M true negatives. FPR is therefore slightly lower than the fraction of non-linked pairs inferred as linked (2 FP / (2 n_0 + M) instead of FP / n_0, with n_0 the number of non-linked pairs).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default true_adjacency array_like

Ground-truth binary (0/1) adjacency matrix, shape (M, M).

required inferred_adjacency array_like

Inferred binary (0/1) adjacency matrix, shape (M, M).

required

Returns:

Name Type Description tpr float

TP / (TP + FN), or NaN if the true network has no links.

fpr float

FP / (FP + TN), or NaN if the true network has no non-links.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If either matrix has entries other than 0 and 1 (a weighted network), or the two have different shapes.

Source code in complex_network_dynamics/network_inference.py 
def tpr_fpr(true_adjacency, inferred_adjacency):
  """True and false positive rates of an inferred network.

  The two matrices are compared entry by entry over the whole M x M matrix,
  as in the thesis code (`TPR_FPR.m`): each link of a symmetric network is
  counted twice, and the diagonal, which is 0 in both, adds M true negatives.
  FPR is therefore slightly lower than the fraction of non-linked pairs
  inferred as linked (2 FP / (2 n_0 + M) instead of FP / n_0, with n_0 the
  number of non-linked pairs).

  Parameters
  ----------
  true_adjacency : array_like
      Ground-truth binary (0/1) adjacency matrix, shape (M, M).
  inferred_adjacency : array_like
      Inferred binary (0/1) adjacency matrix, shape (M, M).

  Returns
  -------
  tpr : float
      TP / (TP + FN), or NaN if the true network has no links.
  fpr : float
      FP / (FP + TN), or NaN if the true network has no non-links.

  Raises
  ------
  ValueError
      If either matrix has entries other than 0 and 1 (a weighted network),
      or the two have different shapes.
  """
  for name, matrix in (("true_adjacency", true_adjacency), ("inferred_adjacency", inferred_adjacency)):
    values = np.unique(np.asarray(matrix, dtype=float))
    if not np.all(np.isin(values, (0.0, 1.0))):
      raise ValueError(
        f"{name} must be binary (0 for no link, 1 for a link); got values {values[:5]}. TPR and FPR "
        "are defined for binary networks: for a weighted network, pass (W != 0).astype(int)."
      )
  if np.shape(true_adjacency) != np.shape(inferred_adjacency):
    raise ValueError(
      f"The matrices have different shapes: {np.shape(true_adjacency)} and {np.shape(inferred_adjacency)}."
    )
  A = np.asarray(true_adjacency) == 1
  B = np.asarray(inferred_adjacency) == 1
  A0 = np.asarray(true_adjacency) == 0
  B0 = np.asarray(inferred_adjacency) == 0
  tp = np.sum(B & A)
  fp = np.sum(B & A0)
  tn = np.sum(B0 & A0)
  fn = np.sum(B0 & A)
  tpr = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn > 0 else np.nan
  fpr = fp / (fp + tn) if fp + tn > 0 else np.nan
  return tpr, fpr

Double-normalised MIR.

The MIR is normalised twice (thesis code double_normalised_MIR.m). Each node's data are first scaled to [0, 1]. def double_normalised_mir(Dat, true_network=None):
  """Double-normalised MIR.

  The MIR is normalised twice (thesis code `double_normalised_MIR.m`). Each
  node's data are first scaled to [0, 1]. Then, for each grid size from
  `Grid`, the MIR of all pairs is min-max scaled, so the pair with the
  smallest MIR gets 0 and the pair with the largest gets 1. The scaled
  matrices are summed over the grid sizes and divided by their largest entry.

  Parameters
  ----------
  Dat : array_like
      Time series, shape (npts, M), with at least three nodes.
  true_network : array_like, optional
      Ground-truth binary (0/1) adjacency matrix, shape (M, M). If given, the
      best reconstruction rate over thresholds 0.01, 0.02, ..., 1 is returned.

  Returns
  -------
  normalised_MIR : np.ndarray
      Symmetric (M, M) matrix with values up to 1; diagonal 0.
  max_rate : float or None
      Largest reconstruction percentage, 100 - 100 * (mismatched entries) /
      (number of links counted in both directions), floored at 0.
      None if `true_network` is not given.

  Raises
  ------
  ValueError
      If `Dat` is not an (npts, M) array with at least three nodes, a node's
      time series is constant, or `true_network` is not a binary (M, M)
      matrix with at least one link.
  """
  Dat = _check_series(Dat, "double_normalised_mir")
  M = Dat.shape[1]
  A = None if true_network is None else _check_true_network(true_network, M)
  span = Dat.max(axis=0) - Dat.min(axis=0)
  if np.any(span == 0):
    raise ValueError(
      f"Node(s) {np.flatnonzero(span == 0).tolist()} have a constant time series, which cannot be "
      "scaled to [0, 1] and carries no information about links."
    )
  Dat = np.ascontiguousarray((Dat - Dat.min(axis=0)) / span)
  pi, pj = np.triu_indices(M, k=1)
  N_min, N_max = Grid(Dat)

  total = np.zeros((M, M))
  for N in range(N_min, N_max + 1):
    mi, t = _pairs_mi_and_decay(Dat, pi, pj, N)
    I_c = np.zeros((M, M))
    I_c[pi, pj] = mi / t
    total += _rescale_upper(I_c, guard_equal=True)

  normalised = total / total.max()
  normalised = normalised + normalised.T

  if A is None:
    return normalised, None
  rates = np.empty(100)
  for k in range(1, 101):
    adj = normalised.copy()
    adj[pi, pj] = adj[pj, pi] = normalised[pi, pj] >= k / 100
    rates[k - 1] = 100 - np.sum(np.abs(adj - A) == 1) * (100 / A.sum())
  return normalised, max(rates.max(), 0.0)

def lagged_double_mir(Dat, max_lag):
  """Lagged, double-normalised MIR.

  For each pair, the MI is the largest MI over time lags -max_lag..max_lag,
  divided by the zero-lag correlation decay time, then min-max scaled and
  summed over grid sizes as in `double_normalised_mir`.

  The grid-size rule differs slightly from `Grid`: its search continues while the average points per cell
  equals the number of occupied cells, and N_max is not capped at 30.

  Parameters
  ----------
  Dat : array_like
      Time series, shape (npts, M), with at least three nodes.
  max_lag : int
      Largest lag, in time steps; 0 uses no lag. Must be smaller than npts.

  Returns
  -------
  lagged_MI : np.ndarray
      Symmetric (M, M) matrix of the largest lagged MI, summed (not averaged)
      over grid sizes.
  lagged_MIR : np.ndarray
      Symmetric (M, M) double-normalised MIR, values up to 1.

  Raises
  ------
  ValueError
      If `Dat` is not an (npts, M) array with at least three nodes, or
      `max_lag` is not a whole number between 0 and npts - 1.
  """
  Dat = np.ascontiguousarray(_check_series(Dat, "lagged_double_mir"))
  M = Dat.shape[1]
  if max_lag != int(max_lag) or not 0 <= max_lag < Dat.shape[0]:
    raise ValueError(
      f"max_lag must be a whole number of time steps between 0 and npts - 1 = {Dat.shape[0] - 1}; "
      f"got {max_lag}."
    )
  pi, pj = np.triu_indices(M, k=1)

  N_final = _grid_sizes_per_pair(Dat, pi, pj, True)
  mean_N = np.mean(N_final)
  N_min = int(np.floor(0.1 * mean_N + 0.5)) + 1
  N_max = int(np.floor(mean_N + 0.5))
  if N_max <= 2:
    N_max *= 2
  if N_min <= 2:
    N_min *= 2

  total_mir = np.zeros((M, M))
  total_mi = np.zeros((M, M))
  for N in range(N_min, N_max + 1):
    mi, t = _pairs_lagged_mi_and_decay(Dat, pi, pj, N, int(max_lag))
    I_s = np.zeros((M, M))
    I_c = np.zeros((M, M))
    I_s[pi, pj] = mi
    I_c[pi, pj] = mi / t
    total_mir += _rescale_upper(I_c, guard_equal=False)
    total_mi += I_s

  lagged_MIR = total_mir / total_mir.max()
  return total_mi + total_mi.T, lagged_MIR + lagged_MIR.T

def best_case_tpr_fpr(similarity_matrix, true_adjacency):
  """ROC sweep over thresholds and the best threshold.

  Every pairwise similarity (minus 1e-12) is tried as a threshold; entries
  above it count as links. The best threshold is the one closest to the
  perfect point (FPR, TPR) = (0, 1). The whole matrix is
  counted, diagonal included, and an upper-triangular input is made symmetric.

  Parameters
  ----------
  similarity_matrix : array_like
      (M, M) similarity matrix, e.g. MIR. Its diagonal is ignored.
  true_adjacency : array_like
      (M, M) ground-truth binary (0/1) adjacency matrix.

  Returns
  -------
  roc : np.ndarray
      Shape (M(M-1)/2, 4), one row per threshold from high to low: TPR, FPR,
      distance to (0, 1), threshold.
  best : np.ndarray
      The rows of `roc` with the smallest distance.
  inferred : np.ndarray
      Inferred adjacency matrix at the best threshold (the smallest one if
      several are equally good): pairs with similarity at least the threshold.

  Raises
  ------
  ValueError
      If `similarity_matrix` is not square, the two matrices have different
      shapes, or `true_adjacency` is not binary.
  """
  S = np.array(similarity_matrix, dtype=float)
  A = np.asarray(true_adjacency)
  M = len(S)
  if S.ndim != 2 or S.shape != (M, M) or M < 2:
    raise ValueError(f"similarity_matrix must be square, (M, M) with M >= 2; got shape {S.shape}.")
  if A.shape != S.shape:
    raise ValueError(f"The matrices have different shapes: similarity {S.shape}, true network {A.shape}.")
  tpr_fpr(A, A)  # raises if the true network is not binary
  np.fill_diagonal(S, 0)
  if np.array_equal(S, np.triu(S)):
    S = S + S.T
  upper = np.triu_indices(M, k=1)
  thresholds = np.sort(S[upper])[::-1] - 1e-12

  roc = np.empty((len(thresholds), 4))
  for k, th in enumerate(thresholds):
    tpr, fpr = tpr_fpr(A, S > th)
    roc[k] = tpr, fpr, np.sqrt((tpr - 1) ** 2 + fpr ** 2), th
  best = roc[roc[:, 2] == roc[:, 2].min()]

  th = best[:, 3].min()
  inferred = S.copy()
  inferred[upper] = S[upper] >= th
  inferred[(upper[1], upper[0])] = inferred[upper]
  return roc, best, inferred
