def plot_similarity_gap_bars(similarity_matrix, true_adjacency, sort_bars=True, title=None):
    """
    Bar chart of the pairwise similarities, coloured by true and false links.

    The grey band marks the thresholds that separate the links from the
    non-links perfectly, if there are any. The figure is shown with
    `plt.show()`.

    Parameters
    ----------
    similarity_matrix : np.ndarray
        (N, N) similarity matrix.
    true_adjacency : np.ndarray
        (N, N) ground-truth binary adjacency matrix.
    sort_bars : bool, optional
        If True, sorts the bars in descending order of similarity. 
        If False, plots them in the original flattened pair index order. Default is True.
    title : str, optional
        Title for the plot. If None, defaults to 'Pairwise Similarities'. Default is None.

    Returns
    -------
    tuple of float or None
        (max_false_sim, min_true_sim): the band of thresholds that separates
        true edges from non-edges perfectly, or None if no such band exists.
    """
    N = similarity_matrix.shape[0]

    # 1. Extract upper triangle (exclude diagonal self-connections)
    triu_indices = np.triu_indices(N, k=1)
    sim_values = similarity_matrix[triu_indices]
    true_edges = (true_adjacency[triu_indices] != 0).astype(int)

    # 2. Apply sorting condition
    if sort_bars:
        sort_idx = np.argsort(sim_values)[::-1]
        plot_sims = sim_values[sort_idx]
        plot_truth = true_edges[sort_idx]
        x_label = "Node Pairs (Ranked highest to lowest similarity)"
    else:
        plot_sims = sim_values
        plot_truth = true_edges
        x_label = "Node Pairs (Unsorted upper-triangle order)"

    # 3. Find the critical boundaries for 100% accuracy
    sim_true = sim_values[true_edges == 1]
    sim_false = sim_values[true_edges == 0]

    min_true_sim = np.min(sim_true) if len(sim_true) > 0 else 0.0
    max_false_sim = np.max(sim_false) if len(sim_false) > 0 else 0.0

    is_perfect_possible = min_true_sim > max_false_sim

    # 4. Plotting
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    x_pos = np.arange(len(plot_sims))

    # Map colors: Green for True Edges, Red for False Edges (Noise/Spurious)
    colors = ['#2ca02c' if truth == 1 else '#d62728' for truth in plot_truth]

    plt.bar(x_pos, plot_sims, color=colors, edgecolor='black', linewidth=0.5, width=1.0)

    # 5. Draw the Grey Threshold Band (or indicate overlap)
    if is_perfect_possible:
        # The grey band where any threshold yields 100% correct inference
        plt.axhspan(max_false_sim, min_true_sim, color='grey', alpha=0.35, 
                    label=f'100% Correct Band\n({max_false_sim:.3f}, {min_true_sim:.3f}]')

        plt.axhline(min_true_sim, color='#2ca02c', linestyle='--', alpha=0.8)
        plt.axhline(max_false_sim, color='#d62728', linestyle='--', alpha=0.8)
    else:
        # If max false is higher than min true, they overlap. Perfect inference is mathematically impossible.
        plt.axhline(min_true_sim, color='#2ca02c', linestyle='--', alpha=0.8, label=f'Min True Edge ({min_true_sim:.3f})')
        plt.axhline(max_false_sim, color='#d62728', linestyle='--', alpha=0.8, label=f'Max False Edge ({max_false_sim:.3f})')

    # Formatting
    plot_title = title if title is not None else "Pairwise Similarities"
    plt.title(plot_title, fontsize=13, fontweight='bold', pad=12)
    plt.ylabel("Similarity Value", fontsize=11)
    plt.xlabel(x_label, fontsize=11)

    # Custom Legend
    legend_elements = [
        Patch(facecolor='#2ca02c', edgecolor='black', label='Ground-Truth Edge'),
        Patch(facecolor='#d62728', edgecolor='black', label='Spurious Connection')
    ]
    handles, labels = plt.gca().get_legend_handles_labels()
    plt.legend(handles=legend_elements + handles, loc='upper right', frameon=True)

    # Remove x-ticks since it's just an index of pairs
    plt.xticks([]) 
    plt.xlim(-0.5, len(plot_sims) - 0.5)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    if is_perfect_possible:
        return (max_false_sim, min_true_sim)
    else:
        print("Warning: Topologies overlap. No threshold can perfectly reconstruct the network.")
        return None

def Grid(Dat):
  """Range of grid sizes [N_min, N_max] for `MIR`, from the occupancy of the cells.

  For each pair of nodes, the largest grid size N is found whose average
  number of points per cell, npts / N^2, is not more than the number of
  occupied cells; N_max is the mean of these sizes and N_min about a tenth of
  it, as in the thesis code (`MIR.m`).

  Parameters
  ----------
  Dat : array_like
      Time series, shape (npts, M): one column per node.

  Returns
  -------
  N_min, N_max : int
      Smallest and largest grid size to use in `MIR` (N_max is capped at 30).
  """
  Dat = np.ascontiguousarray(Dat, dtype=np.float64)
  M = Dat.shape[1]
  pi, pj = np.triu_indices(M, k=1)
  N_final = _grid_sizes_per_pair(Dat, pi, pj)

  mean_N = np.mean(N_final)
  # Round halves up; np.round would send 0.5 to 0
  N_min = int(np.floor(0.1 * mean_N + 0.5)) + 1
  N_max = int(np.floor(mean_N + 0.5))

  if N_max <= 2:
    N_max *= 2
  if N_min <= 2:
    N_min *= 2
  if N_max > 30:
    N_max = 30
  if N_min > N_max:
    N_min = N_max

  return N_min, N_max

def corr_decay(Dat, gridsize):
  """Correlation decay time for every pair of nodes.

  For each pair, the joint trajectory is binned on a `gridsize` x `gridsize`
  grid and the cell-to-cell transitions form a graph. The largest shortest
  path in that graph estimates how long correlations take to decay.

  Parameters
  ----------
  Dat : array_like
      Time series, shape (npts, M).
  gridsize : int
      Number of cells per axis.

  Returns
  -------
  np.ndarray
      Symmetric (M, M) matrix of decay times. The diagonal holds the decay
      time of each node paired with itself, which `MIR` uses.
  """
  Dat = np.ascontiguousarray(Dat, dtype=np.float64)
  M = Dat.shape[1]
  pi, pj = np.triu_indices(M)
  _, decay = _pairs_mi_and_decay(Dat, pi, pj, int(gridsize))

  decay_matrix = np.zeros((M, M))
  decay_matrix[pi, pj] = decay
  decay_matrix[pj, pi] = decay
  return decay_matrix

def calculate_distance_metrics(G, mode="giant"):
    """Diameter and average shortest path length of a network that may be disconnected.

    NetworkX's `diameter` and `average_shortest_path_length` raise an error
    when the network is not connected, because some distances are infinite.
    This function restricts both to the pairs of nodes that can reach each
    other. For a connected network it returns the NetworkX values.

    Parameters
    ----------
    G : networkx.Graph
        Undirected network.
    mode : {"giant", "all"}, optional
        What to do when the network is not connected. "giant" (default) uses
        the largest connected component only. "all" returns the largest
        diameter over all components, and the average shortest path length
        over every pair of nodes that can reach each other.

    Returns
    -------
    diameter : int
        Longest shortest path. 0 if the network has no links.
    avg_path_length : float
        Average shortest path length. 0.0 if the network has no links.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `mode` is not "giant" or "all", or `G` is directed.
    """
    if mode not in ("giant", "all"):
        raise ValueError(f"mode must be 'giant' or 'all'; got '{mode}'.")
    if G.is_directed():
        raise ValueError("G must be undirected; for a directed network, pass G.to_undirected().")
    if len(G) == 0:
        return 0, 0.0

    # Case 1: Fully connected graph
    if nx.is_connected(G):
        if len(G) <= 1:
            return 0, 0.0
        return nx.diameter(G), nx.average_shortest_path_length(G)

    # Filter connected components that have at least 2 nodes
    components = [
        G.subgraph(c).copy() for c in nx.connected_components(G) if len(c) > 1
    ]

    # Handle edge case: no edges exist in the graph (all isolated nodes)
    if not components:
        return 0, 0.0

    # Case 2: Unconnected - Giant Component Mode (Standard)
    if mode == "giant":
        giant = max(components, key=len)
        return nx.diameter(giant), nx.average_shortest_path_length(giant)

    # Case 3: Unconnected - Aggregate Across All Components Mode
    else:
        # Global diameter is the maximum diameter found in any component
        diam = max(nx.diameter(c) for c in components)

        # Weighted average shortest path length over all connected pairs
        total_reachable_pairs = 0
        weighted_path_sum = 0.0

        for c in components:
            n_c = len(c)
            pairs_c = n_c * (n_c - 1) / 2
            l_c = nx.average_shortest_path_length(c)

            weighted_path_sum += l_c * pairs_c
            total_reachable_pairs += pairs_c

        avg_path = (
            (weighted_path_sum / total_reachable_pairs)
            if total_reachable_pairs > 0
            else 0.0
        )
        return diam, avg_path

docs.title: Surrogate Data
docs.text:
Surrogate datasets keep some properties of the data and destroy others. Comparing a measure such as MIR on the data with its values on many surrogates tells you whether the measured dependence is real.

All generators take time series as an (n_points, n_nodes) array and return (n_surrogates, n_points, n_nodes). Pass rng (a seed or numpy.random.Generator) for reproducible results.

Function Keeps Destroys amplitude_phase_surrogates Range of amplitudes and phases Amplitude correlation and phase synchronisation (fractions pc_amplitude, pc_phase of time points) phaseran Power spectrum of each node and linear cross-correlations Nonlinear structure random_surrogates Shape only Everything correlated_random_surrogates A fixed correlation between all pairs Everything else

docs.title: Amplitude-phase modulated surrogate data (APMSD)
docs.text:
Each node's analytic signal is computed with the Hilbert transform:

\[ z(t) = x(t) + i\,\mathcal{H}[x](t) = A(t)\, e^{i\theta(t)} \]

In each surrogate, a random fraction pc_amplitude of the time points get amplitudes drawn uniformly from \([\min A, \max A]\), and a separate random fraction pc_phase get phases drawn uniformly from \([\min\theta, \max\theta]\). The surrogate is \(\mathrm{Re}\big[\tilde A(t)\, e^{i\tilde\theta(t)}\big]\).

The surrogate is the real part of the modified signal. Randomising amplitudes removes amplitude correlation between nodes; randomising phases removes phase synchronisation.

As in the thesis code (HT_mix_A_theta), the randomised time points are the same for all nodes, while every node gets its own new values; the smallest and largest amplitude and phase are taken over all nodes together; and the Hilbert transform is applied to the data as given, with the mean left in (unlike hilbert_phases, which removes it by default).

def amplitude_phase_surrogates(data, n_surrogates=1, pc_amplitude=1.0, pc_phase=0.5, rng=None):
    """Amplitude-phase modulated surrogate data (APMSD).

    Each node's analytic signal A(t) exp(i theta(t)) is computed with the
    Hilbert transform. In every surrogate, a random fraction `pc_amplitude` of
    the time points get new amplitudes drawn uniformly between the smallest
    and largest amplitude in the data, and a separate random fraction
    `pc_phase` get new phases drawn uniformly between the smallest and largest
    phase. The surrogate is the real part of the modified signal. Randomising
    amplitudes removes amplitude correlation between nodes; randomising phases
    removes phase synchronisation.

    As in the thesis code (`HT_mix_A_theta`), the randomised time points are
    the same for all nodes, while every node gets its own new values; the
    smallest and largest amplitude and phase are taken over all nodes
    together; and the Hilbert transform is applied to the data as given, with
    the mean left in (unlike `hilbert_phases`, which removes it by default).

    Parameters
    ----------
    data : array_like
        Time series, shape (n_points, n_nodes).
    n_surrogates : int, optional
        Number of surrogate datasets. Default is 1.
    pc_amplitude : float, optional
        Fraction of time points whose amplitudes are randomised, in [0, 1].
        Default is 1.
    pc_phase : float, optional
        Fraction of time points whose phases are randomised, in [0, 1].
        Default is 0.5.
    rng : numpy.random.Generator or int, optional
        Random generator or seed.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Surrogates, shape (n_surrogates, n_points, n_nodes).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `data` is not two-dimensional, or a fraction is outside [0, 1].
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(rng)
    data = _check_data(data)
    n_points, n_nodes = data.shape
    for name, pc in (("pc_amplitude", pc_amplitude), ("pc_phase", pc_phase)):
        if not 0 <= pc <= 1:
            raise ValueError(f"{name} is a fraction of the time points and must be between 0 and 1; got {pc}.")

    analytic = hilbert(data, axis=0)
    amplitude = np.abs(analytic)
    phase = np.angle(analytic)
    amp_min, amp_max = amplitude.min(), amplitude.max()
    ph_min, ph_max = phase.min(), phase.max()
    n_amp = int(np.ceil(pc_amplitude * n_points))
    n_ph = int(np.ceil(pc_phase * n_points))

    surrogates = np.empty((n_surrogates, n_points, n_nodes))
    for k in range(n_surrogates):
        new_amplitude = amplitude.copy()
        rows = rng.permutation(n_points)[:n_amp]
        new_amplitude[rows] = rng.random((n_amp, n_nodes)) * (amp_max - amp_min) + amp_min

        new_phase = phase.copy()
        rows = rng.permutation(n_points)[:n_ph]
        new_phase[rows] = rng.random((n_ph, n_nodes)) * (ph_max - ph_min) + ph_min

        surrogates[k] = np.real(new_amplitude * np.exp(1j * new_phase))
    return surrogates

The same random phases are added to every column's Fourier transform (Prichard & Theiler, 1994), so each surrogate keeps the power spectrum of every node and the linear correlations between nodes, but destroys any nonlinear structure. The thesis code calls this surrogate type twnsd.

def phaseran(data, n_surrogates=1, rng=None):
    """Phase-randomised surrogates that keep the cross-correlations.

    The same random phases are added to every column's Fourier transform
    (Prichard & Theiler, 1994), so each surrogate keeps the power spectrum of
    every node and the linear correlations between nodes, but destroys any
    nonlinear structure. The thesis code calls this surrogate type `twnsd`.

    Parameters
    ----------
    data : array_like
        Time series, shape (n_points, n_nodes). If n_points is even, the last
        sample is dropped.
    n_surrogates : int, optional
        Number of surrogate datasets. Default is 1.
    rng : numpy.random.Generator or int, optional
        Random generator or seed.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Surrogates, shape (n_surrogates, n_frames, n_nodes), where n_frames is
        n_points rounded down to an odd number.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(rng)
    data = _check_data(data)
    n_frames, n_nodes = data.shape
    if n_frames < 3:
        raise ValueError(f"data needs at least 3 time points to randomise its Fourier phases; got {n_frames}.")
    if n_frames % 2 == 0:
        n_frames -= 1
        data = data[:n_frames]

    half = (n_frames - 1) // 2
    spectrum = np.fft.fft(data, axis=0)

    surrogates = np.empty((n_surrogates, n_frames, n_nodes))
    for k in range(n_surrogates):
        phases = np.exp(2j * np.pi * rng.random(half))[:, None]
        randomised = spectrum.copy()
        randomised[1:half + 1] *= phases
        randomised[half + 1:] *= np.conj(phases[::-1])
        surrogates[k] = np.real(np.fft.ifft(randomised, axis=0))
    return surrogates

def correlated_random_surrogates(data, n_surrogates=1, correlation=0.5, n_points=None, rng=None):
    """Gaussian surrogates with the same correlation between every pair of nodes.

    Standard normal samples multiplied by the Cholesky factor of a matrix with
    ones on the diagonal and `correlation` elsewhere. The thesis code
    (`corr_randsd`) always made 1000 points; here the surrogates are as long
    as the data unless `n_points` is given.

    Parameters
    ----------
    data : array_like
        Time series, shape (n_points, n_nodes); only its shape is used.
    n_surrogates : int, optional
        Number of surrogate datasets. Default is 1.
    correlation : float, optional
        Correlation between every pair of nodes, above -1/(n_nodes - 1) and
        below 1. Default is 0.5.
    n_points : int, optional
        Length of each surrogate. Default is the length of the data.
    rng : numpy.random.Generator or int, optional
        Random generator or seed.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Surrogates, shape (n_surrogates, n_points, n_nodes).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `data` is not two-dimensional, or no set of nodes can have the
        requested correlation between every pair.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(rng)
    data_points, n_nodes = _check_data(data).shape
    n_points = data_points if n_points is None else int(n_points)
    lowest = -1.0 / (n_nodes - 1) if n_nodes > 1 else -1.0
    if not lowest < correlation < 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"correlation must be above {lowest:.3g} (= -1/(n_nodes - 1)) and below 1 for {n_nodes} nodes; "
            f"got {correlation}."
        )
    R = np.full((n_nodes, n_nodes), correlation)
    np.fill_diagonal(R, 1.0)
    upper = np.linalg.cholesky(R).T  # Upper Cholesky factor
    return rng.standard_normal((n_surrogates, n_points, n_nodes)) @ upper

docs.title: Synchronisation
docs.text:
Measures of how synchronised the nodes of a network are. Phases and time series are (n_points, n_nodes) arrays.

Function Measures hilbert_phases Instantaneous phases \(\theta_i(t)\) from the Hilbert transform global_sync Running average of the Kuramoto order parameter pairwise_sync Phase locking between every pair of nodes global_order Synchrony \(R(t)\) of Rubido et al. deviation_from_sync Average distance between two oscillators over time

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
Kuramoto order parameter (global_sync returns its running average):

\[ \rho(t) = \frac{1}{M}\Big|\sum_{j=1}^{M} e^{i\theta_j(t)}\Big| \]

Pairwise phase synchronisation (Gómez-Gardeñes et al., 2010):

\[ r_{ij} = \Big|\big\langle e^{i(\theta_i(t)-\theta_j(t))}\big\rangle_t\Big| \]

Global order (Rubido et al.): the variance over time of the network average \(\bar x(t)\), divided by the average over nodes of each node's variance over time:

\[ R(t) = \frac{\langle \bar x^2\rangle_t - \langle \bar x\rangle_t^2}{\frac{1}{M}\sum_i \big(\langle x_i^2\rangle_t - \langle x_i\rangle_t^2\big)} \]

All three are 1 for fully synchronised nodes.

Deviation from synchronisation: the running average of \(|x_2 - x_1|\), which goes to zero when two oscillators synchronise completely.

docs.title: Phases of signals with a nonzero mean
docs.text: hilbert_phases subtracts each node's mean before the Hilbert transform (demean=True). The phase is the angle of \(x(t) + i\,\mathcal{H}[x](t)\) seen from the origin, and the transform of a constant is zero, so an offset moves the whole orbit away from the origin: for maps on \([0, 1]\) the angle hardly moves, and uncoupled nodes look synchronised (two independent logistic maps give \(r_{12} \approx 0.49\) instead of \(\approx 0\)). For signals that oscillate around zero, such as the Lorenz \(x\), demeaning changes nothing. The thesis and the paper used the raw signals; pass demean=False to reproduce their values.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from complex_network_dynamics import load_network, stochastic_kuramoto, global_sync, pairwise_sync

A = load_network("16nodes")
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
w = rng.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi, 16)
t, phases = stochastic_kuramoto(rng.random(16) * 2 * np.pi, A, w, K=10, D=1, dt=0.01, n_steps=20_000, rng=1)

global_sync(phases)[-1]   # overall synchrony
pairwise_sync(phases)     # 16 x 16 matrix

hilbert_phases(data, demean=True)

Instantaneous phases from the Hilbert transform.

The phase is the angle of the analytic signal x(t) + i Hx, measured from the origin. The Hilbert transform of a constant is zero, so a signal with a nonzero mean gives an orbit shifted away from the origin, and for a large offset (e.g. maps on [0, 1]) the angle hardly moves: uncoupled nodes then look phase-synchronised. Subtracting each node's mean first removes this artefact and changes nothing for signals that oscillate around zero.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data array_like

Time series, shape (n_points, n_nodes).

required demean bool

Subtract each node's mean before the transform. Default is True. Use False to reproduce the thesis and Yildirim & Antonopoulos (2024), e.g. rho = 0.93 for the 4 logistic maps in Table 1.

True

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

Unwrapped phase of each node's analytic signal, same shape as data.

def hilbert_phases(data, demean=True):
    """Instantaneous phases from the Hilbert transform.

    The phase is the angle of the analytic signal x(t) + i H[x](t), measured
    from the origin. The Hilbert transform of a constant is zero, so a signal
    with a nonzero mean gives an orbit shifted away from the origin, and for a
    large offset (e.g. maps on [0, 1]) the angle hardly moves: uncoupled nodes
    then look phase-synchronised. Subtracting each node's mean first removes
    this artefact and changes nothing for signals that oscillate around zero.

    Parameters
    ----------
    data : array_like
        Time series, shape (n_points, n_nodes).
    demean : bool, optional
        Subtract each node's mean before the transform. Default is True.
        Use False to reproduce the thesis and Yildirim & Antonopoulos (2024),
        e.g. rho = 0.93 for the 4 logistic maps in Table 1.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Unwrapped phase of each node's analytic signal, same shape as `data`.
    """
    data = np.asarray(data, dtype=float)
    if demean:
        data = data - data.mean(axis=0)
    return np.unwrap(np.angle(hilbert(data, axis=0)), axis=0)

def global_sync(phases):
    """Running average of the Kuramoto order parameter.

    The order parameter at time t is

        rho(t) = |sum_j exp(i theta_j(t))| / M,

    which is 1 when all phases are equal and near 0 when they are spread out.

    Parameters
    ----------
    phases : array_like
        Phases, shape (n_points, M).

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Shape (n_points,): the mean of rho over the first 1, 2, ..., n_points
        time points.
    """
    phases = np.asarray(phases, dtype=float)
    rho = np.abs(np.exp(1j * phases).sum(axis=1)) / phases.shape[1]
    return np.cumsum(rho) / np.arange(1, len(rho) + 1)

def pairwise_sync(phases):
    """Phase synchronisation between every pair of nodes.

    r_ij = |mean_t exp(i (theta_i(t) - theta_j(t)))| (Gomez-Gardenes et al., 2010),
    1 for phase-locked nodes and near 0 for independent ones.

    Parameters
    ----------
    phases : array_like
        Phases, shape (n_points, M).

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Symmetric (M, M) matrix with ones on the diagonal.
    """
    phases = np.asarray(phases, dtype=float)
    z = np.exp(1j * phases)
    return np.abs(z.T @ np.conj(z)) / len(phases)

R(t) is the variance over time of the network average, divided by the network average of each node's variance over time, both computed from the first t points. It is 1 for fully synchronised nodes and near 1/M for independent ones.

def global_order(data):
    """Synchronisation measure R(t) of Rubido et al.

    R(t) is the variance over time of the network average, divided by the
    network average of each node's variance over time, both computed from
    the first t points. It is 1 for fully synchronised nodes and near 1/M for
    independent ones.

    Parameters
    ----------
    data : array_like
        Time series, shape (n_points, M).

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Shape (n_points,). The first value is undefined (the variance of a
        single point, 0/0) and returned as NaN.
    """
    X = np.asarray(data, dtype=float)
    t = np.arange(1, len(X) + 1)
    x_avg = X.mean(axis=1)
    numerator = np.cumsum(x_avg**2) / t - (np.cumsum(x_avg) / t) ** 2
    node_var = np.cumsum(X**2, axis=0) / t[:, None] - (np.cumsum(X, axis=0) / t[:, None]) ** 2
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
        return numerator / node_var.mean(axis=1)

def deviation_from_sync(x1, x2):
    """Running average distance between two oscillators.

        E_i = (1 / i) sum_{k=1}^{i} |x2_k - x1_k|,   i = 1, ..., n

    E goes to zero when the two oscillators synchronise completely.

    Parameters
    ----------
    x1, x2 : array_like
        Time series of the two oscillators, of equal length n.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Shape (n,): the average of |x2 - x1| over the first 1, 2, ..., n points.

    Notes
    -----
    The thesis MATLAB code (`deviation_from_sync.m`, used for Fig. 4.3(e))
    divided the running sum by the time t_i instead of the number of points,
    which gives the average only for a unit step starting at t = 0 (for a step
    h it is 1/h times too large), and dropped the last two points.
    """
    x1 = np.asarray(x1, dtype=float).ravel()
    x2 = np.asarray(x2, dtype=float).ravel()
    if x1.shape != x2.shape:
        raise ValueError(f"x1 and x2 must have the same length, got {x1.size} and {x2.size}")
    return np.cumsum(np.abs(x2 - x1)) / np.arange(1, x1.size + 1)

docs.title: Introduction to Network Theory
docs.text:
In [1]: Copied! 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import networkx as nx import numpy as np

Figure 1: (a) The seven bridges of Königsberg, where uppercase letters denote the land masses and lowercase letters the bridges. (b) Its graphical representation, where the land masses , B, C\( and \) are the vertices and the bridges the connecting lines, referred to as edges, what is called a graph in mathematics.

Euler reformulated the question as a graphical problem. He assigned the uppercase letters \(A, B, C\) and \(D\) to the land masses (referred to as vertices or nodes) and the lowercase letters \(a, b, c, d, e, f\) and \(g\) to the bridges (referred to as edges or links). In 1736, he proved that there is no way to cross every bridge exactly once.

Euler's solution was both simple and elegant: he counted the number of bridges connected to each land mass, which we now call the degree of a node. For example, there are three bridges connecting \(B\) (or \(C\)) to the others, and the degrees of the nodes \(A, B, C\) and \(D\) are \(5, 3, 3\) and \(3\), respectively. Whenever a walk enters a node through one bridge it has to leave it through another, so every node must have an even degree, except possibly the two nodes where the walk starts and ends. Hence, such a walk can exist only if zero or two nodes have an odd degree. Here all four nodes have an odd degree, therefore, there is no way to cross all the bridges exactly once.

This brings us to the mathematical definition of a graph [3].

Definition (Graph). A graph \(G\) is an ordered triple \((V(G), E(G), \psi_{G})\) consisting of a non-empty set \(V(G)\) of vertices, a set \(E(G)\), disjoint from \(V(G)\), of edges, and an incidence function \(\psi_{G}\) that associates with each edge of \(G\) an unordered pair of (not necessarily distinct) vertices of \(G\). If \(e\) is an edge and \(u\) and \(v\) are vertices such that \(\psi_{G}(e) = uv\), then \(e\) is said to join \(u\) and \(v\); the vertices \(u\) and \(v\) are called the ends of \(e\).

For the problem of the Königsberg bridges, the components of the graph are

\[ \begin{aligned} G &= (V(G), E(G), \psi_{G}), \text{ where}\\ V(G) &= \{A, B, C, D\}, \\ E(G) &= \{a, b, c, d, e, f, g\},\\ \psi_{G}(a) &= AB,\ \psi_{G}(b) = AB,\ \psi_{G}(c) = AC,\ \psi_{G}(d) = AC,\\ \psi_{G}(e) &= AD,\ \psi_{G}(f) = BD,\ \psi_{G}(g) = CD. \end{aligned} \]

We can build this graph with NetworkX, from the list of bridges used for Figure 1(b), and repeat Euler's argument. Two bridges join \(A\) and \(B\), and two join \(A\) and \(C\), so we need a MultiGraph, which allows more than one link between the same pair of nodes.

Figure 3: (a) A triangle of the regular network: three nodes that are all linked to each other. (b) An open triplet: a node (the centre) together with two of its neighbours that are not linked to each other (dashed line). If the dashed link existed, the triplet would be closed and the three nodes would form a triangle.

Every triangle closes three triplets, one centred at each of its nodes, hence

\[ T = \frac{3 \times \text{number of triangles}}{\text{number of triplets}}, \]

\[ \text{number of triangles} = \frac{1}{6}\,\mathrm{Tr}\big(A^{3}\big), \qquad \text{number of triplets} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\binom{d_i}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i (d_i - 1), \]

where \(d_{i}\) is the degree of node \(i\). The entry \((A^{3})_{ii}\) counts the closed routes of length 3 that start and end at node \(i\); each triangle is counted six times in the trace, as it can start at any of its three nodes and be traversed in two directions.

(b) The local clustering coefficient considers the links among the neighbours of a node, and was introduced in [5] to quantify the small-worldness of a network. For a node \(i\) with degree \(d_{i} \ge 2\),

\[ C_{i} = \frac{2 e_{i}}{d_{i}(d_{i}-1)}, \]

where \(e_{i}\) is the number of links among the neighbours of node \(i\), in other words, the number of triangles that include node \(i\), \(e_{i} = (A^{3})_{ii}/2\). For a node with fewer than two neighbours we set \(C_{i} = 0\). The mean local clustering coefficient is the average over all the nodes,

\[ C = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} C_{i}. \]

Note: the two formulas are similar, but they are not the same. The transitivity divides the total number of closed triplets by the total number of triplets of the whole network at once, whereas \(C\) computes this ratio node by node and then takes the average. They coincide when all nodes have the same degree, as in a regular network.

docs.title: Introduction to Network Theory¶
docs.text:
Every method in this library works on a network: a set of nodes and the links between them. In this tutorial we introduce the vocabulary used in all the later ones, following Chapter 2 (Sections 2.1 and 2.2) of the PhD thesis [1].

You will learn:

  1. where graph theory comes from, and how a graph is defined;
  2. how to store a network in an adjacency matrix and read the degrees of its nodes from it;
  3. how to compute the shortest path lengths, the average path length and the diameter;
  4. how to compute the global and the local clustering coefficients, by hand and with NetworkX.

docs.title: The Birth of Graph Theory¶
docs.text: The history of graph theory in mathematical problem solving dates back to 1736 [2]. Swiss-born mathematician Leonhard Euler, who was working in St. Petersburg at the time, encountered a question that was famous among the people of the Prussian city of Königsberg (now Kaliningrad): could one walk through the city crossing each of its bridges exactly once? The river Pregel divides the city into four land masses, which were connected by seven bridges (Figure 1).

docs.title: The 1875 Bridge¶
docs.text: In 1875 a new bridge, which we call \(h\), was built between the land masses \(B\) and \(C\). It adds 1 to the degrees of \(B\) and \(C\), so they become \(5, 4, 4\) and \(3\) for \(A, B, C\) and \(D\). Now only two nodes, \(A\) and \(D\), have an odd degree, and, by Euler's argument, a walk that crosses every bridge exactly once becomes possible: it has to start at one of the two odd nodes and end at the other. We add the bridge to our graph, check it again, and let NetworkX find such a walk.

docs.title: Graph Theory to Network Science¶
docs.text:
The authors in [4] discussed the distinction between the terms "graph" and "network", which are commonly used interchangeably in the scientific literature. However, the difference lies in that a graph refers to the schematic visualisation used to solve a mathematical problem, whereas a network refers to the graphical representation of a real-life problem, such as transportation maps, social interactions, protein-protein interactions, etc.

Despite their close relationship, we shall henceforth refer to them as "networks" and to their components, vertices and edges, as "nodes" and "links", respectively.

docs.title: Regular Network¶
docs.text:
If all the \(n\) nodes of a network have the same degree \(d\), it is called a regular network (or \(d\)-regular network). Every link adds 1 to the degree of each of its two ends, so the sum of all degrees, \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_{i} = n d\), is twice the number of links and must be an even number. Moreover, \(d \le n - 1\), since a node can be connected to at most \(n - 1\) other nodes.

Below, we generate a random 3-regular network with 6 nodes (\(n d = 18\), which is even).

docs.title: The Adjacency Matrix¶
docs.text: A network with \(n\) nodes can be stored in an \(n \times n\) adjacency matrix \(A\), where \(A_{ij} = 1\) if nodes \(i\) and \(j\) are linked and \(A_{ij} = 0\) otherwise. For an undirected network \(A\) is symmetric, and the sum of row \(i\) is the degree of node \(i\), \(d_{i} = \sum_{j} A_{ij}\). Hence, the sum of all the entries of \(A\) equals \(n d = 18\) for our network.

docs.title: Degree Distribution¶
docs.text: The degree distribution shows how many nodes have each degree. In a regular network there is only one column, as the degrees of all nodes are equal. The network types of the next tutorial differ mainly in the shape of this distribution.

docs.title: Shortest Path Length¶
docs.text:
A path in a network is a sequence of links that connects two nodes. For instance, \(P_1 = 1 \to 3 \to 2 \to 4\) is a path between nodes \(1\) and \(4\) traversing along nodes \(3\) and \(2\). The path length is the number of links traversed along the path, so \(|P_1| = 3\) for this path. The shortest path length between two nodes is the smallest length among all the paths that connect them.

The shortest path lengths of all pairs of nodes form the matrix \(\mathcal{D}\), which we can compute from the powers of the adjacency matrix \(A\). The entry \((A^{k})_{ij}\) is the number of ways to go from node \(i\) to node \(j\) in exactly \(k\) steps:

\[ \begin{aligned} A_{ij} &= \text{the number of routes of length 1 between nodes } i \text{ and } j,\\ (A^{2})_{ij} &= \text{the number of routes of length 2 between nodes } i \text{ and } j,\\ &\ \ \vdots \\ (A^{n-1})_{ij} &= \text{the number of routes of length } n-1 \text{ between nodes } i \text{ and } j. \end{aligned} \]

Such a route may visit the same node more than once (it is called a walk), but the shortest one never does. Hence, the shortest path length \(\mathcal{D}_{ij}\) is the smallest \(k\) for which \((A^{k})_{ij} > 0\). In a network with \(n\) nodes a shortest path has at most \(n - 1\) links, so it is enough to compute the powers up to \(A^{n-1}\).

Algorithm: shortest path lengths of all pairs from matrix powers

Input: the adjacency matrix \(A\) of an unweighted network with \(n\) nodes. Output: the matrix of shortest path lengths \(\mathcal{D}\).

  1. Set every entry of \(\mathcal{D}\) to \(\infty\), and the diagonal to \(0\).
  2. Set \(A_{k} = I\), the \(n \times n\) identity matrix.
  3. For \(k = 1, 2, \dots, n - 1\):
    • multiply \(A_{k}\) by \(A\), so that \(A_{k} = A^{k}\);
    • for every pair \((i, j)\) with \(\mathcal{D}_{ij} = \infty\) and \((A_{k})_{ij} > 0\), set \(\mathcal{D}_{ij} = k\);
    • stop if no entry of \(\mathcal{D}\) equals \(\infty\), as all the distances have been found.
  4. Return \(\mathcal{D}\). An entry that is still \(\infty\) belongs to a pair of nodes with no path between them.

This algorithm is easy to follow but slow for large networks; for faster ones, see the NetworkX documentation.

docs.title: Average Path Length and Diameter¶
docs.text:
The average shortest path length, \(\bar{d}\), is the mean of the shortest path lengths across the network,

\[ \bar{d} = \frac{1}{n (n-1)}\sum_{i \neq j} \mathcal{D}_{ij}. \]

The diameter, \(R\), of a network is the maximum of the shortest path lengths across all pairs of nodes, namely the greatest entry of the matrix \(\mathcal{D}\).

docs.title: Clustering Coefficients¶
docs.text:
The clustering coefficient measures how often two neighbours of a node are themselves linked, so that the three nodes form a triangle. There are two types of clustering coefficients in the literature.

(a) The global clustering coefficient, also known as transitivity, considers the connected triplets of nodes, where a triplet is a node together with two of its neighbours (a path of length 2 centred at that node). It is the fraction of triplets that are closed by a third link. Figure 3 shows the difference on our regular network.

docs.title: The Same Metrics with NetworkX¶
docs.text: NetworkX has a function for each of these metrics, and they agree with the values we computed by hand. Note that average_shortest_path_length and diameter raise an error when the network is not connected, because some distances are then infinite; the function calculate_distance_metrics of the library handles that case, and we use it in the next tutorial.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• A graph is a set of nodes, a set of links and a rule that says which nodes each link joins. Euler's argument on the Königsberg bridges only needs the degrees of the nodes.
  • The adjacency matrix \(A\) stores a network; its row sums are the degrees, and its powers count the routes of a given length between two nodes.
  • The matrix of shortest path lengths \(\mathcal{D}\) gives the average path length (its mean) and the diameter (its greatest entry).
  • The transitivity \(T\) and the mean local clustering coefficient \(C\) both measure how many triangles a network has, the first for the whole network at once and the second node by node.

In the next tutorial we use these metrics to compare regular, random, small-world and scale-free networks.

docs.text:
1. H. Yıldırım, Network Inference Using Information-theoretical Approaches, Statistical Hypothesis Tests, and The Amplitude-Phase Modulated Surrogate Data Method, PhD thesis, University of Essex (2024), Chapter 2. https://repository.essex.ac.uk/39296/
  2. A.-L. Barabási, Linked: How Everything Is Connected to Everything Else and What It Means for Business, Science, and Everyday Life, Basic Books (2003).
  3. J. A. Bondy and U. S. R. Murty, Graph Theory with Applications, Macmillan (1976).
  4. M. Pósfai and A.-L. Barabási, Network Science, Cambridge University Press (2016).
  5. D. J. Watts and S. H. Strogatz, Collective dynamics of 'small-world' networks, Nature 393, 440–442 (1998).

These are the references of Chapter 2 of the thesis [1].

In the ring lattice with \(n = 40\) and \(k = 8\), every node is linked to its 4 nearest neighbours on each side, so one step along a link moves at most \(k/2 = 4\) positions around the ring. The node farthest from any given node is the one opposite to it, \(n/2 = 20\) positions away, which takes \(20/4 = 5\) steps to reach; hence, the diameter is \(D = 5\). Most pairs of nodes are much closer than this, and averaging the distance over all pairs gives \(\langle L \rangle \approx 2.95\).

The clustering, on the other hand, is high: the neighbours of a node are themselves close to each other on the ring, so most of them are also linked. By counting the links among the \(k\) neighbours of a node, one finds that, as long as the network is not too small compared with \(k\), the clustering coefficient of a ring lattice depends only on \(k\),

\[ C = \frac{3(k-2)}{4(k-1)}, \]

which gives \(C = 18/28 \approx 0.643\) for \(k = 8\), the value we obtained above. Note that the average clustering coefficient and the transitivity coincide, since every node has the same degree and the same neighbourhood. Thus, the ring lattice has highly clustered neighbourhoods but, as we see next, long paths between distant nodes.

Figure 2: Diameter, \(D\) (red squares), and average shortest path length, \(\langle L \rangle\) (blue circles), of ring lattices with \(k = 8\), as in Fig. 1, over the network size, \(n = 9, 10, \dots, 49\). At \(n = 40\), the two curves give the values of the ring lattice of Fig. 1, \(D = 5\) and \(\langle L \rangle = 2.95\).

The plot shows the price of having only local links. With \(k = 8\), as in Fig. 1, one step moves at most \(k/2 = 4\) positions around the ring, and the farthest node is about \(n/2\) positions away, so the diameter is \(D = \lceil \lfloor n/2 \rfloor / (k/2) \rceil \approx n/k\). Hence, the diameter increases by one each time \(k = 8\) nodes are added (at \(n = 18, 26, 34\) and \(42\)), which gives the staircase shape, and for \(n = 40\) it is \(D = 5\), the value we computed above for the network of Fig. 1. The average shortest path length, on the other hand, grows smoothly, approximately as \(n/(2k) + 1/2\), which gives \(\langle L \rangle \approx 3\) for \(n = 40\), close to the exact value of 2.95 above. In other words, the distances in a ring lattice grow linearly with the network size, as in Fig. 2.3(c) of the thesis [1]. This is not what one observes in most real networks, which have short paths despite their large size, and it is the motivation for the small-world network below.

All four networks have the same number of nodes, \(N = 40\), and a comparable number of links: 160 in the ring lattice and the Watts–Strogatz network, about 160 in the Erdős–Rényi network (156 on average), and 144 in the Barabási–Albert network, so that the average degree is close to 8 in all of them. As in the thesis [1], we choose the same size and a comparable density because both affect network inference, and these are the networks used in Chapter 5 to compare inference across topologies. Hence, the differences in the table come from how the links are arranged, not from how many there are.

  • Distances. The ring lattice has the largest diameter, \(D = 5\), and the longest average shortest path, \(\langle L \rangle = 2.95\), since all its links are local. Rewiring only 10% of the links in the Watts–Strogatz network creates shortcuts across the ring, which shorten the paths, while the random and scale-free networks, which have no local structure at all, have the shortest paths, \(\langle L \rangle \approx 2\). In the scale-free network, most of the shortest paths between nodes that are not linked pass through one of the hubs, so that its diameter is only 3.
  • Clustering. The ring lattice also has the highest clustering, \(C = 0.64\), as we saw above. The Watts–Strogatz network keeps most of it, since most of its links are still local, while in the random network \(C\) is close to the connection probability \(p = 0.2\), because any two neighbours of a node are linked with probability \(p\), independently of everything else. Thus, the small-world network combines the short paths of the random network with the high clustering of the ring lattice, which is the small-world property.
  • Average clustering versus transitivity. In the first three networks, the two measures are almost equal, as all nodes have similar degrees. In the scale-free network, the average clustering (0.34) is clearly higher than the transitivity (0.25): the many nodes with few links have a high local clustering coefficient, while the hubs, which take part in most of the triplets and hence dominate the transitivity, have a low one.

Note that the values of the Erdős–Rényi and Watts–Strogatz networks change slightly from run to run, as a new random network is drawn each time. Moreover, 40 nodes make a small network, so the differences between the models are smaller than they would be for large networks; we kept this size, as in the thesis [1], because of the computational cost of network inference in Chapter 5.

docs.title: Network Types¶
docs.text:
In the previous tutorial we introduced the measures that describe the structure of a network: the degree distribution, the average shortest path length, the diameter and the clustering coefficients. In this tutorial, we use them to compare four of the best-known network models, following Section 2.3 of the PhD thesis [1]:

  • the ring lattice, a regular network in which every node is linked to its nearest neighbours;
  • the Erdős–Rényi random network, in which any two nodes are linked with the same probability [2];
  • the Watts–Strogatz small-world network, a ring lattice with a few randomly rewired links [3];
  • the Barabási–Albert scale-free network, which grows by preferential attachment [4].

For each of them, we generate a network with 40 nodes and a comparable number of links, plot it together with its degree distribution, and compute its structural measures with calculate_distance_metrics of the library. Finally, we compare the four networks in one table, as in Table 2.1 of the thesis, and through their adjacency matrices. These networks of 40 nodes are the ones used in Chapter 5 of the thesis to study how the network structure affects network inference.

You will learn:

  1. how each of the four models is constructed, and with which parameters;
  2. why their degree distributions differ: a single column for the ring lattice, a binomial distribution for the random network and a power law for the scale-free network;
  3. how a few rewired links make the shortest paths of the small-world network much shorter than in the ring lattice, while its clustering stays far higher than in a random network.

docs.title: Ring Lattice¶
docs.text: A ring lattice (RL) belongs to the family of regular networks, meaning that all nodes have the same degree, \(d_{i} = k\) for all \(i\); such a network is called a \(k\)-regular network. In addition, in a ring lattice the nodes are placed on a circle, and every node is linked to its \(k/2\) nearest neighbours on each side. The ring lattice is the starting point of the Watts–Strogatz model [3], and it is obtained from that model with rewiring probability \(p = 0\), which is how we generate it below.

docs.title: Random Networks¶
docs.text:
Random networks, which were introduced by Paul Erdős and Alfréd Rényi in the early 1960s [2], have the same probability of drawing a link between any two nodes. For a network with \(N\) nodes and \(n\) links, the number of networks that can be constructed is the number of ways of choosing \(n\) links out of all \(N(N-1)/2\) possible links, namely \(\binom{N(N-1)/2}{n}\). Equivalently, we can link each pair of nodes with probability \(p\), and then the degree \(k\) of any node follows the binomial distribution

\[ P(k) = \binom{N-1}{k}\, p^{k} (1-p)^{N-1-k}. \]

docs.title: Small World Network¶
docs.text:
As we see in the ring lattice, the shortest path length depends on the network size, and it increases as \(N\) rises. However, most real networks, despite their often large size, have a relatively short average path length between any two nodes. This property was first investigated in a social network inferred from Milgram's experiment. In his experiment, randomly selected individuals in Nebraska were asked to forward a letter to a distant target individual if they knew them, based on provided information such as the name, occupation and approximate location. If they did not know the target, they were instructed to send the letter to someone who might know the person. Milgram then tracked the path of the letters and, surprisingly, found that on average the letters reached the target individual after only 6 deliveries.

This shows that a network might have a relatively small mean shortest path length even if it involves many nodes. This is known as the small-worldness of a network, and it helps one to characterise the network at hand. Brain networks and the World Wide Web (WWW) are frequently classified as small-world networks, because some links connect different clusters within these systems, significantly speeding up the transmission of information.

Watts and Strogatz [3] showed similarities in the neural network of Caenorhabditis elegans, the power grid of the western US and the collaboration network of film actors. They developed an algorithm to generate a small-world (SW) network, which has two parameters: the number of neighbours and the probability of rewiring. The algorithm starts with a ring lattice, in which all nodes are connected to a given number of nearest neighbours, and each link is rewired with the given probability. Since some nodes are then connected to distant nodes, this increases the connectivity of the network and eventually gives it the small-world property.

docs.title: Scale-Free Network¶
docs.text:
Traditionally, the ER model has been used extensively to study complex networks, assuming an equal connection probability for all nodes. However, the analyses of large real networks show that the degree distribution of most of them follows a power law instead of a binomial distribution (or a Poisson distribution for large networks). Albert-László Barabási and Réka Albert analysed the topological structure of real-world networks, such as the WWW and the citation network of scientific articles, and they showed that the nodes with higher degrees tend to have a higher connection probability, which is called preferential attachment. Based on these observations, they devised an algorithm to generate scale-free (SF) networks, known as the BA model [4]. There are two generic mechanisms underlying the algorithm:

  1. Growth: new nodes join the network at each iteration.
  2. Preferential attachment: the probability that a new node is linked to an existing node depends on the number of links the existing node already has.

In such networks, the degree distribution decays as a power law, \(p(k) \sim k^{-\gamma}\).

Preferential attachment ⇒ the rich get richer, the poor stay poor

docs.title: Adjacency Matrices¶
docs.text: Before comparing the four networks through their structural measures, we look at their adjacency matrices. In the ring lattice, every node is linked to its nearest neighbours, so the links form a band along the diagonal (and in the corners, where the ring closes). Rewiring a few links in the Watts–Strogatz network scatters a few dots away from the band, while the Erdős–Rényi and Barabási–Albert networks have no band at all; in the latter, the first nodes, which collect the most links, form dense rows and columns.

docs.title: Comparison of Network Topologies¶
docs.text: Finally, we collect the structural measures of the four networks in one table, as in Table 2.1 of the thesis [1].

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
In this tutorial, we generated four network models with 40 nodes and comparable numbers of links, and compared their structure:

  • the ring lattice, in which all nodes have the same degree and only local links, has high clustering but long paths, which grow linearly with the network size;
  • the Erdős–Rényi random network has a binomial degree distribution, short paths and low clustering, close to the connection probability \(p\);
  • the Watts–Strogatz small-world network, obtained by rewiring a small fraction of the links of a ring lattice, has short paths while keeping most of the clustering of the lattice;
  • the Barabási–Albert scale-free network, which grows by preferential attachment, has a heavy-tailed degree distribution with a few hubs, which keep the paths short.

These are the network types used in Chapter 5 of the thesis [1] to study how the structure of a network affects network inference. In the next tutorial, we move from the structure of networks to the dynamics on them, starting with discrete maps.

def bifurcation(f, r_values, n_transient=1000, n_keep=300, **params):
    """Points visited by x -> f(x, r) after the transient, for every r at once.

    Returns an array of shape (n_keep, len(r_values)).
    """
    x = np.full(len(r_values), 0.4)
    for _ in range(n_transient):
        x = f(x, r=r_values, **params)
    orbit = np.empty((n_keep, len(r_values)))
    for n in range(n_keep):
        x = f(x, r=r_values, **params)
        orbit[n] = x
    return orbit

def lyapunov_exponent(f, df, r_values, n_transient=1000, n_average=5000, **params):
    """Lyapunov exponent of x -> f(x, r): the average of log|f'(x)| along the orbit, for every r at once."""
    x = np.full(len(r_values), 0.4)
    for _ in range(n_transient):
        x = f(x, r=r_values, **params)
    total = np.zeros(len(r_values))
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore"):  # log(0) = -inf when the orbit sits exactly where f' = 0
        for _ in range(n_average):
            total += np.log(np.abs(df(x, r=r_values, **params)))
            x = f(x, r=r_values, **params)
    return total / n_average


def plot_bifurcation_and_exponent(r_values, orbit, exponent, title, exponent_range):
    fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
    ax1.plot(r_values, orbit.T, "k,", alpha=0.3, rasterized=True)
    ax1.set_xlim(r_values[0], r_values[-1])
    ax1.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax1.set_xlabel("Parameter $r$")
    ax1.set_ylabel("$x$")

    ax2 = ax1.twinx()
    ax2.plot(r_values, exponent, color="red", linewidth=0.8)
    ax2.axhline(0, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
    ax2.set_ylim(exponent_range)
    ax2.set_ylabel(r"Lyapunov exponent $\lambda$", color="red")
    ax2.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor="red")
    plt.title(title)
    plt.show()

docs.title: Discrete Maps: from One Map to a Network¶
docs.text:
The simplest dynamical systems in the library are discrete maps: a rule \(x_{n+1} = f(x_n)\) that is applied again and again. In this tutorial we study the two maps used in Yıldırım & Antonopoulos (2024) [1], the logistic map and the circle map, first on their own and then coupled on a network, following Chapter 3 (Sections 3.1 to 3.3) of the PhD thesis [2]. The data generated here are the ones from which the networks are inferred in the later tutorials.

You will learn:

  1. how the logistic map goes from a fixed point to chaos as its parameter \(r\) grows, and how to draw its bifurcation diagram;
  2. what a Lyapunov exponent is, and how it tells chaotic from regular behaviour;
  3. how the circle map behaves, and why we use \(r = 0.35\);
  4. how to couple maps on a network with simulate_discrete_models, and how to compute their Lyapunov spectrum (Table 3.2 of the thesis).

docs.title: 1. The Logistic Map¶
docs.text:
The logistic map, popularised by Robert May in 1976 [3], is a model of a population that grows when it is small and shrinks when it is crowded,

\[ x_{n+1} = r\, x_n (1 - x_n), \]

where \(x_n \in [0, 1]\) is the population at iteration \(n\), which plays the role of discrete time, and \(r \in [0, 4]\) is the growth rate. This is Eq. (14) of the paper and Eq. (3.6) of the thesis, and cnd.logistic in the library.

The sequence \(x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots\) is called a trajectory or orbit. Its long-term behaviour depends on \(r\):

  • for \(r = 2\) the trajectory ends at \(x = 0.5\), a fixed point, namely a point that satisfies \(f(x) = x\). Indeed, \(2x(1 - x) = x\) gives \(x = 0\) or \(x = 0.5\);
  • for \(r = 3.4\) it jumps between two points for ever (a period-2 orbit);
  • for \(r = 4\) it never repeats itself: the map is chaotic.

We plot the three cases below, starting from the same initial condition \(x_0 = 0.4\).

docs.title: 2. Bifurcation Diagram of the Logistic Map¶
docs.text:
To see all the values of \(r\) at once, we iterate the map for each \(r\), discard the first iterations (the transient) and plot the points the trajectory visits afterwards. This is the bifurcation diagram (Fig. 3.5 of the thesis).

For \(r \in (1, 3)\), the trajectories converge to a fixed point. As \(r\) increases from 3, one observes period 2, period 4, period 8, and so on: the period doubles again and again, and the doublings come closer and closer to each other. If the \(n\)th doubling occurs at \(r = r_n\), the ratio \((r_n - r_{n-1}) / (r_{n+1} - r_n)\) tends to the Feigenbaum constant, \(\delta \approx 4.6692\), which is the same for a large family of maps. The orbits become chaotic around \(r = 3.57\). An emergence of period-3 behaviour is observed around \(r = 3.83\), followed by a rapid return to irregularity.

cnd.logistic accepts arrays, so we iterate all the values of \(r\) together.

docs.title: 3. Lyapunov Exponent of a Map¶
docs.text:
The bifurcation diagram shows where the map looks irregular; the Lyapunov exponent measures it. Two trajectories that start a small distance \(\epsilon\) apart are, after one iteration, about \(|f'(x)|\,\epsilon\) apart. The Lyapunov exponent is the average of the logarithm of this growth rate along the trajectory (Section 3.2.1 of the thesis; see also [4]),

\[ \lambda = \lim_{k \to \infty} \frac{1}{k} \sum_{n=1}^{k} \log |f'(x_n)|. \]

If \(\lambda > 0\), nearby trajectories separate exponentially fast, as \(\epsilon\, e^{\lambda n}\), so the system is sensitive to its initial condition, which is the signature of chaos. If \(\lambda < 0\), they approach each other and the behaviour is regular (a fixed point or a periodic orbit).

For the logistic map, \(f'(x) = r(1 - 2x)\), which is cnd.df_logistic. For \(r = 4\) the exact value is known, \(\lambda = \log 2 \approx 0.693\). Below, we compute \(\lambda\) for every \(r\) and plot it over the bifurcation diagram, as in Fig. 3.9(a) of the thesis.

docs.title: 4. The Circle Map¶
docs.text:
The second map of the paper is the circle map (Eq. (15) of the paper, Eq. (3.12) of the thesis),

\[ x_{n+1} = x_n + r - \frac{K}{2\pi} \sin(2\pi x_n) \pmod 1, \]

where \(x_n \in [0, 1)\), \(r \in [0, 1]\) is a parameter and \(K = 6.9115\). In the library it is cnd.circle, with the derivative \(f'(x) = 1 - K\cos(2\pi x)\) in cnd.df_circle. We repeat the same analysis, which gives Fig. 3.9(b) of the thesis.

docs.title: 5. Coupled Maps on a Network¶
docs.text:
So far every map evolved on its own. To generate data from a network, we place one map on every node and let each node feel its neighbours (Eq. (13) of the paper, Eq. (3.13) of the thesis),

\[ x^{i}_{n+1} = (1 - \alpha)\, f(x^{i}_{n}, r) + \frac{\alpha}{k_i} \sum_{j=1}^{M} A_{ij}\, f(x^{j}_{n}, r), \]

where \(x^{i}_{n}\) is the \(n\)th iteration of node \(i\), \(M\) the number of nodes, \(A\) the adjacency matrix of the network, \(k_i\) the degree of node \(i\) and \(\alpha \in [0, 1]\) the coupling strength. For \(\alpha = 0\) the nodes are independent, and as \(\alpha\) grows each node follows the average of its neighbours more and more.

The library ships with the two networks used in the thesis (Fig. 3.10): one with 12 nodes and 14 links, and one with 16 nodes and 26 links. We load them with cnd.load_network.

docs.title: 6. Lyapunov Spectrum of Coupled Maps¶
docs.text:
A system of \(M\) coupled maps has \(M\) Lyapunov exponents, \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_M\), called the Lyapunov spectrum: one average growth rate for each independent direction in which a small perturbation can point (Section 3.2.2 of the thesis). To compute them, following the algorithm of [5, 6], simulate_discrete_models evolves \(M\) orthonormal vectors with the Jacobian matrix of the coupled system at every iteration, orthonormalises them again, and averages the logarithms of their growth. Following the definition in [4], a bounded orbit is chaotic if it is not asymptotically periodic, no exponent is exactly zero and at least one exponent is positive.

Table 3.2 of the thesis lists the spectra of the 16 coupled logistic and circle maps for \(\alpha = 0.1\). We compare them with the ones we have just computed.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• The logistic map goes from a fixed point to chaos through period doublings as \(r\) grows; the circle map shows similar dynamics. We use \(r = 4\) and \(r = 0.35\), respectively, where both are chaotic.
  • The Lyapunov exponent is the average of \(\log|f'(x_n)|\) along a trajectory. It is positive for chaotic behaviour and negative for regular behaviour.
  • cnd.simulate_discrete_models couples any map on any network and returns the trajectory and the Lyapunov spectrum; with the 16-node network and \(\alpha = 0.1\) it reproduces Table 3.2 of the thesis.

In the next tutorial we move from maps to systems of differential equations.

docs.title: Integrating ODEs: Euler, Runge-Kutta and Lyapunov Exponents
docs.text:
In [2]: Copied! 
def euler_method(f, y0, t0, h, n_steps, **params):
    """Integrate dy/dt = f(t, y) with the Euler method; returns the times and the states."""
    t_vals = t0 + h * np.arange(n_steps + 1)
    y_vals = np.empty((n_steps + 1, len(y0)))
    y_vals[0] = y0
    for n in range(n_steps):
        y_vals[n + 1] = y_vals[n] + h * f(t_vals[n], y_vals[n], **params)
    return t_vals, y_vals
def euler_method(f, y0, t0, h, n_steps, **params): """Integrate dy/dt = f(t, y) with the Euler method; returns the times and the states.""" t_vals = t0 + h * np.arange(n_steps + 1) y_vals = np.empty((n_steps + 1, len(y0))) y_vals[0] = y0 for n in range(n_steps): y_vals[n + 1] = y_vals[n] + h * f(t_vals[n], y_vals[n], **params) return t_vals, y_vals In [3]: Copied!

n_steps_lv = 10_000            # total time = n_steps * h = 100

The oscillations grow from one cycle to the next, and the curve in the phase portrait spirals outwards instead of closing. This is not a property of the model but the truncation error of the Euler method accumulating at every step. We quantify it with \(V\) after introducing a better method.

In [4]: Copied! 
def conserved_quantity(y, alpha=1.1, beta=0.4, delta=0.1, gamma=0.4):
    x, p = y[:, 0], y[:, 1]
    return delta * x - gamma * np.log(x) + beta * p - alpha * np.log(p)


t_rk4, lv_rk4 = cnd.rk4_with_lyapunov(cnd.lotka_volterra, y0_lv, 0.0, h_lv, n_steps_lv + 1,
                                      lyap_mode="none", n_transient=0)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))
ax1.plot(lv_euler[:, 0], lv_euler[:, 1], color="purple", linewidth=0.8, label="Euler")
ax1.plot(lv_rk4[:, 0], lv_rk4[:, 1], color="black", linewidth=1.2, label="RK4")
ax1.set_xlabel("Prey $x$")
ax1.set_ylabel("Predator $p$")
ax1.set_title(f"Phase portrait, $h = {h_lv}$")
ax1.legend()

V0 = conserved_quantity(y0_lv[None, :])[0]
ax2.semilogy(t_euler[1:], np.abs(conserved_quantity(lv_euler) - V0)[1:], color="purple", label="Euler")
ax2.semilogy(t_rk4[1:], np.abs(conserved_quantity(lv_rk4) - V0)[1:], color="black", label="RK4")
ax2.set_xlabel("Time $t$")
ax2.set_ylabel("$|V(t) - V(0)|$")
ax2.set_title("Error in the conserved quantity")
ax2.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Error in V at t = 100:  Euler {abs(conserved_quantity(lv_euler)[-1] - V0):.2e},  "
      f"RK4 {abs(conserved_quantity(lv_rk4)[-1] - V0):.2e}")

Error in V at t = 100:  Euler 2.40e-01,  RK4 8.56e-10

With the same step size, the RK4 solution closes on itself and keeps \(V\) constant many orders of magnitude better than the Euler solution. To reach a similar accuracy, the Euler method would need a far smaller step size, and, consequently, far more steps.

In [5]: Copied! 
y0_lorenz = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0])
h = 0.005
n_steps = 40_000      # recorded time = n_steps * h = 200
n_transient = 2_000   # the first 10 time units are discarded

t_lorenz, traj_lorenz, lyap_times, lyap_history = cnd.rk4_with_lyapunov(
    cnd.lorenz, y0_lorenz, 0.0, h, n_steps, df=cnd.lorenz_jacobian,
    lyap_mode="history", n_transient=n_transient, qr_interval=5,
)

for k, colour in enumerate(["tab:red", "tab:green", "tab:blue"]):

The trajectory draws the butterfly-shaped Lorenz attractor, and the three exponents settle to one positive, one zero and one negative value.

We now compare the two methods for the same step size, \(h = 0.005\). In the thesis, the maximum Lyapunov exponent of the Lorenz system approaches \(0.9029\) as time increases (Fig. 3.12(b)). There is also an exact check: the sum of the exponents equals the average divergence of \(f\), which for the Lorenz system is the constant \(-(\sigma + 1 + \beta) = -13.6667\).

In [6]: Copied! 
rows = {}

for name, integrator in [("Euler", cnd.euler_with_lyapunov), ("RK4", cnd.rk4_with_lyapunov)]:
    _, _, spectrum = integrator(cnd.lorenz, y0_lorenz, 0.0, h, n_steps, df=cnd.lorenz_jacobian,
                                n_transient=n_transient, qr_interval=5)
    rows[f"{name}, h = {h}"] = spectrum

lorenz_table = pd.DataFrame(rows, index=["λ1", "λ2", "λ3"]).T
lorenz_table["Sum"] = lorenz_table.sum(axis=1)
lorenz_table.round(4)
rows = {} for name, integrator in [("Euler", cnd.euler_with_lyapunov), ("RK4", cnd.rk4_with_lyapunov)]: _, _, spectrum = integrator(cnd.lorenz, y0_lorenz, 0.0, h, n_steps, df=cnd.lorenz_jacobian, n_transient=n_transient, qr_interval=5) rows[f"{name}, h = {h}"] = spectrum lorenz_table = pd.DataFrame(rows, index=["λ1", "λ2", "λ3"]).T lorenz_table["Sum"] = lorenz_table.sum(axis=1) lorenz_table.round(4) Out[6]: λ1 λ2 λ3 Sum Euler, h = 0.005 0.9428 0.0049 -14.7709 -13.8232 RK4, h = 0.005 0.9027 -0.0067 -14.5626 -13.6667

Both methods give a chaotic orbit, but the Euler method misses the sum of the exponents in the first decimal, while RK4 reproduces it and gives a \(\lambda_1\) close to the \(0.9029\) of the thesis. Note that the running estimates above still fluctuate after 200 time units, so a longer trajectory is needed for more digits.

For the Lotka-Volterra model both exponents are zero, since its orbits are closed curves and nearby orbits neither separate nor approach each other exponentially.

Number of nodes: 12   size of the state vector: 36

The system now has \(3M = 36\) dimensions and a \(36 \times 36\) Jacobian matrix, so the cost of the integration matters. We integrate it for 50 time units, after a transient of 10, with the four integrators of the library and measure their running time:

  • cnd.euler_with_lyapunov, with \(h = 2 \times 10^{-4}\), as the Euler method needs a small step;
  • cnd.rk4_with_lyapunov, with \(h = 10^{-3}\);
  • the compiled RK4 solver made by cnd.build_rk4_lyapunov, with the same \(h\). It uses the same method as rk4_with_lyapunov, but the model and the solver are compiled to machine code with Numba. It needs the compiled versions of the model, cnd.coupled_lorenz_njit and cnd.coupled_lorenz_jacobian_njit, and takes the parameters as one tuple args;
  • cnd.solve_ivp_with_lyapunov (RK45), recording the state every 0.05 time units.
In [9]: Copied! 
t_record, t_discard = 50.0, 10.0
params = dict(A=A, K=K, sigma=10.0, rho=28.0, beta=8 / 3)
results = []


def record(method, step, runtime, spectrum):
    results.append({"Method": method, "Step size": step, "Running time (s)": round(runtime, 2),
                    "λ1": round(spectrum[0], 3), "Positive exponents": int(np.sum(spectrum > 0.1))})


# Euler
h_euler = 2e-4
start = time.perf_counter()
_, _, spectrum_euler = cnd.euler_with_lyapunov(
    cnd.coupled_lorenz, y0_coupled, 0.0, h_euler, int(t_record / h_euler), df=cnd.coupled_lorenz_jacobian,
    n_transient=int(t_discard / h_euler), qr_interval=25, **params)
record("Euler", f"h = {h_euler}", time.perf_counter() - start, spectrum_euler)

# RK4

start = time.perf_counter()
_, _, spectrum_rk4 = cnd.rk4_with_lyapunov(
    cnd.coupled_lorenz, y0_coupled, 0.0, h_rk4, int(t_record / h_rk4), df=cnd.coupled_lorenz_jacobian,
    n_transient=int(t_discard / h_rk4), qr_interval=5, **params)
record("RK4", f"h = {h_rk4}", time.perf_counter() - start, spectrum_rk4)

# Compiled RK4: the first call compiles the solver, so we time the second one

# RK45

_, _, spectrum_rk45_coupled = cnd.solve_ivp_with_lyapunov(

The running times depend on the computer, but their order does not: the compiled RK4 solver is the fastest, several times faster than the same method in plain Python, which is why we recommend it for long simulations of large networks. The values of \(\lambda_1\) agree only roughly between the methods, because 50 time units are too short for the exponents of a 36-dimensional chaotic system to converge; what the methods agree on is that the system is chaotic, with about one positive exponent per node.

Finally, we look at the trajectory of the compiled solver: the attractor of one node, the Lyapunov spectrum and the \(x\) variable of all the nodes over time.

Each node switches between the two wings of its own attractor (yellow and purple bands) at its own times: with \(K = 0.2\) the nodes are coupled, but far from synchronised. Whether the links can be recovered from such data is the subject of the tutorials on correlation and mutual information and on MIR and APMSD.

docs.title: Integrating ODEs: Euler, Runge-Kutta and Lyapunov Exponents¶
docs.text:
In the previous tutorial time advanced in steps. The continuous models of the library (Lorenz, Rössler, Hindmarsh-Rose, Kuramoto) are systems of ordinary differential equations (ODEs), which have to be solved numerically. In this tutorial we introduce the numerical integration methods of the library, following Sections 3.1.1, 3.2.2 and 3.3.2 of the PhD thesis [1], and use them on the Lorenz system of Yıldırım & Antonopoulos (2024) [2].

You will learn:

  1. how the Euler and the 4th-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) methods work, and how much their accuracy differs for the same step size;
  2. how the Lyapunov exponents of a system of ODEs are computed together with its trajectory;
  3. how an adaptive method (RK45) chooses its own step size;
  4. how to simulate Lorenz systems coupled on a network, and which integrator of the library to choose.

docs.title: 1. ODEs and Numerical Errors¶
docs.text:
Systems of ODEs are often challenging to solve analytically; therefore, numerical integration methods are commonly used to calculate their trajectories [3]. The general form of an ordinary differential equation is

\[ \dot{y} = f(t, y), \qquad y(t_{0}) = y_{0}, \]

where \(\dot{y}\) is the time derivative of the variable \(y\), \(f(t, y)\) the function that defines the system and \(y_0\) the initial condition. Let the analytical solution of the system be \(F_{t}\) and its numerical approximation \(Y_{t}\) at time \(t\). A numerical method advances the solution in steps of size \(h\), and makes two kinds of error:

  • the truncation error, which comes from the method itself. The error made in one step is called the local truncation error, and the error accumulated up to time \(t\), \(E(t) = F_{t} - Y_{t}\), the global truncation error. Both become smaller as \(h\) decreases;
  • the round-off error, which arises because computers carry out every operation with finite precision. It grows with the number of steps, so \(h\) cannot be made arbitrarily small.

docs.title: 2. The Euler Method¶
docs.text:
The fundamental technique to approximate the solution of a system of ODEs is the Euler method. It uses the Taylor series expansion of the solution,

\[ y(t + h) = y(t) + h\, \dot{y}(t) + \frac{h^{2}}{2!} \ddot{y}(t) + \frac{h^{3}}{3!} y^{(3)}(t) + \ldots, \]

and keeps its first two terms only. Since \(\dot{y} = f(t, y)\), this gives

\[ y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h f(t_n, y_{n}), \]

where \(h\) is the step size. The method follows the slope at the beginning of the step for the whole step. The neglected terms start with \(h^2\), so the local truncation error is of order \(h^2\) and the global one of order \(h\): halving the step size only halves the error.

Algorithm 1: Euler method

  1. Define \(f(t, y)\) and set the initial values \(t = t_0\), \(y = y_0\).
  2. Choose the step size \(h\) and the number of steps \(n\).
  3. Repeat \(n\) times:
    • \(y \leftarrow y + h f(t, y)\),
    • \(t \leftarrow t + h\).
  4. Return \(t\) and \(y\).

The algorithm takes only a few lines of Python.

docs.title: Example: the Lotka-Volterra (Predator-Prey) Model¶
docs.text:
We test it on the Lotka-Volterra model, a 2-dimensional nonlinear system in which the populations of a prey, \(x\), and of a predator, \(p\), oscillate over time,

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{dx}{dt} &= \alpha x - \beta x p, \\ \frac{dp}{dt} &= \delta x p - \gamma p, \end{aligned} \]

where

  • \(\alpha\) is the growth rate of the prey in the absence of predators,
  • \(\beta\) the predation rate,
  • \(\delta\) the growth rate of the predators per prey eaten,
  • \(\gamma\) the natural death rate of the predators.

In the library this is cnd.lotka_volterra, with the defaults \(\alpha = 1.1\), \(\beta = 0.4\), \(\delta = 0.1\) and \(\gamma = 0.4\). This model is a good test because we know what the exact solution looks like: the quantity

\[ V = \delta x - \gamma \ln x + \beta p - \alpha \ln p \]

stays constant along every solution, so the trajectory in the \((x, p)\) plane is a closed curve that repeats itself for ever. Any change of \(V\) in a numerical solution is, therefore, an error of the method.

docs.title: 3. The 4th-Order Runge-Kutta Method (RK4)¶
docs.text:
The RK4 method is the most widely used member of the family of Runge-Kutta methods. Instead of following the slope at the beginning of the step, it evaluates the slope at four points within the step and combines them, so that the result agrees with the Taylor series expansion up to its 4th-order term:

\[ \begin{aligned} k_1 &= f(t_n, y_n), \\ k_2 &= f\big(t_n + \tfrac{h}{2},\ y_n + \tfrac{h}{2} k_1\big), \\ k_3 &= f\big(t_n + \tfrac{h}{2},\ y_n + \tfrac{h}{2} k_2\big), \\ k_4 &= f(t_n + h,\ y_n + h k_3), \\ y_{n+1} &= y_n + \tfrac{h}{6}\,(k_1 + 2 k_2 + 2 k_3 + k_4). \end{aligned} \]

Its global truncation error is of order \(h^4\): halving the step size makes the error 16 times smaller, at the cost of four evaluations of \(f\) per step instead of one.

The library provides both methods as cnd.euler_with_lyapunov and cnd.rk4_with_lyapunov. They take the same arguments: the function f, the initial state y0, the initial time t0, the step size h and the number of recorded points n_steps. With lyap_mode="none" they return the times and the trajectory only. Below, we integrate the Lotka-Volterra model with RK4, using the same step size as before, and compare the conserved quantity \(V\) of the two solutions.

docs.title: 4. Lyapunov Exponents of a Flow¶
docs.text:
In the previous tutorial, the Lyapunov exponent of a map was the average of \(\log|f'(x_n)|\) along the trajectory. For a system of ODEs the idea is the same (Section 3.2.2 of the thesis, following [4, 5]). A small perturbation \(\delta y\) of the solution evolves according to the variational equation,

\[ \dot{J} = \Lambda(t)\, J, \qquad J(0) = I, \]

where \(\Lambda(t) = Df(y(t))\) is the Jacobian matrix of \(f\) evaluated on the trajectory, and the columns of \(J\) are the perturbation vectors, which start as the unit vectors. Since \(\Lambda(t)\) depends on the state at time \(t\), the system and its variational equation have to be solved simultaneously. The vectors are orthonormalised every few steps (the library uses a QR decomposition, which is equivalent to the Gram-Schmidt process), so that they neither grow without bound nor all collapse onto the most unstable direction. The Lyapunov exponents are the averages of the logarithms of their growth per unit of time, \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_M\), one for each dimension of the system.

A bounded trajectory that is not periodic is chaotic if \(\lambda_1 > 0\) [6]. Moreover, a trajectory of a system of ODEs that does not end at a fixed point always has one exponent equal to zero, which corresponds to a perturbation along the trajectory itself.

docs.title: The Lorenz System¶
docs.text:
We use the system derived by Edward Lorenz as a model of convection in the atmosphere, whose sensitivity to the initial conditions started what is now called chaos theory [7],

\[ \begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= \sigma (y - x), \\ \dot{y} &= x (\rho - z) - y, \\ \dot{z} &= x y - \beta z, \end{aligned} \]

with \(\sigma = 10\), \(\rho = 28\) and \(\beta = 8/3\), which lead to a chaotic orbit (Eq. (3.15) of the thesis). In the library these are cnd.lorenz and its Jacobian matrix cnd.lorenz_jacobian.

To compute the Lyapunov exponents, we pass the Jacobian as df. The first n_transient steps are discarded, so that the trajectory is on the attractor before the averaging starts, and the vectors are orthonormalised every qr_interval steps. With lyap_mode="history" the functions also return the running estimates of the exponents, which show how they converge.

docs.title: 5. Adaptive Runge-Kutta Methods¶
docs.text:
The Euler and RK4 methods use the same step size everywhere, although a solution may change quickly in some parts and slowly in others. Adaptive methods estimate the local truncation error at every step by comparing two Runge-Kutta methods of orders \(p\) and \(p + 1\), and choose the step size so that this error stays below a tolerance: small steps where the solution changes quickly, large steps where it is smooth. The most common one is RK45, based on the Dormand-Prince pair of orders 4 and 5 [8], which is the default of scipy.integrate.solve_ivp and the method used for the continuous systems in the thesis and the paper.

In the library, cnd.solve_ivp_with_lyapunov wraps the SciPy solver. Since the Lyapunov exponents and the later analysis need the solution at equally spaced times, the function integrates over windows of length dt_qr; at the end of each window it records the state and orthonormalises the perturbation vectors. Instead of a number of steps, it takes the total time t_total, and the tolerances rtol and atol.

docs.title: 6. Coupled Lorenz Systems on a Network¶
docs.text:
To generate data from a network, we place one Lorenz system on every node and couple the nodes through their \(x\) variables (Eq. (20) of the paper, Eq. (3.16) of the thesis),

\[ \begin{aligned} \dot{x}_i &= \sigma (y_i - x_i) + K \sum_{j=1}^{M} A_{ij} (x_j - x_i), \\ \dot{y}_i &= x_i (\rho - z_i) - y_i, \\ \dot{z}_i &= x_i y_i - \beta z_i, \end{aligned} \]

where \(K\) is the coupling strength and \(A\) the adjacency matrix of the \(M\) nodes. In the library this is cnd.coupled_lorenz, with the Jacobian matrix cnd.coupled_lorenz_jacobian. The state is one vector of length \(3M\), ordered as \([x_1, \dots, x_M, y_1, \dots, y_M, z_1, \dots, z_M]\).

We use the 12-node network of the library with \(K = 0.2\), the value of the paper, and the initial conditions of the thesis, \(x_i = 0.1 + 0.5\xi_i\), \(y_i = -0.19 + 0.5\xi_i\) and \(z_i = -0.27 + 0.5\xi_i\), where \(\xi_i\) is a uniform random number in \([0, 1]\).

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• The Euler method follows the slope at the beginning of each step and has an error of order \(h\); RK4 combines four slopes and has an error of order \(h^4\). For the same step size, RK4 kept the conserved quantity of the Lotka-Volterra model many orders of magnitude better.
  • The Lyapunov exponents of a system of ODEs are computed by integrating the variational equation together with the system. For the Lorenz system we found one positive, one zero and one negative exponent, whose sum is \(-13.67\).
  • RK45 chooses its own step size to keep the local error below a tolerance.
  • The library offers four integrators with the same interface: euler_with_lyapunov, rk4_with_lyapunov, the compiled build_rk4_lyapunov (the fastest) and solve_ivp_with_lyapunov (adaptive).
