def apmsd_parameter_space(data, true_network, p_sl=0.1, levels=np.linspace(0, 1, 11), rng=None):
    # TPR and FPR for every (pc_amplitude, pc_phase) on the grid; [i, j] is
    # pc_amplitude = levels[i], pc_phase = levels[j]
    rng = np.random.default_rng(rng)
    tpr = np.zeros((len(levels), len(levels)))
    fpr = np.zeros_like(tpr)
    for i, pc1 in enumerate(levels):
        for j, pc2 in enumerate(levels):
            _, _, rates = cnd.mir_surrogate_test(
                data, p_sl=p_sl, true_network=true_network,
                pc_amplitude=pc1, pc_phase=pc2, rng=rng,
            )
            tpr[i, j], fpr[i, j] = rates[0, 1:]
    return tpr, fpr


def plot_parameter_space(tpr, fpr, levels=np.linspace(0, 1, 11), title=None, ax=None):
    # Colour: TPR. Red circles: FPR > 0 (area grows with FPR). Green: perfect inference.
    ax = ax or plt.gca()
    pct = 100 * levels
    image = ax.pcolormesh(pct, pct, tpr.T, cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1, shading="nearest")
    P1, P2 = np.meshgrid(pct, pct, indexing="ij")
    wrong = fpr > 0
    ax.scatter(P1[wrong], P2[wrong], s=400 * fpr[wrong], facecolors="none", edgecolors="red", linewidths=1.5)
    perfect = (tpr == 1) & (fpr == 0)
    ax.scatter(P1[perfect], P2[perfect], s=60, color="limegreen", edgecolors="black")
    ax.set_xlabel("$pc_{1}$, amplitudes randomised (%)")
    ax.set_ylabel("$pc_{2}$, phases randomised (%)")
    ax.set_xticks(pct[::2])
    ax.set_yticks(pct[::2])
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title)
    return image

At 100 Hz (1000 points) many pairs of percentages still recover the chain exactly. At 20 Hz (200 points) none do here, while Fig. 3c of the paper shows success at 20 Hz and even 10 Hz. Taking every 500th point of a chaotic map leaves almost independent samples, and with only 200 of them the MIR estimates are too noisy: the MIR of the linked pairs is no longer clearly above that of their surrogates, so their \(p\)-values are not 0. The paper may have down-sampled differently; the down-sampling script is not in the thesis code, so this part is not a like-for-like comparison.

docs.title: Network Inference with MIR and APMSD¶
docs.text:
This tutorial runs the full method of Yıldırım & Antonopoulos [1] on the first example of the paper (Section 3.2.1): four coupled logistic maps on a chain network. The paper reports exact numbers for this case (Table 2 and Figs. 2 and 3), so every result below can be compared with it.

The method has four steps:

  1. Compute the mutual information rate (MIR) of every pair of nodes.
  2. Generate amplitude-phase modulated surrogate data (APMSD): a fraction \(pc_{1}\) of the instantaneous amplitudes and a fraction \(pc_{2}\) of the instantaneous phases of each signal are replaced by random values.
  3. Test each pair: \(H_0\) says the two nodes are not connected. The \(p\)-value is the fraction of surrogates whose MIR is at least the MIR of the data. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (FDR) corrects for testing many pairs at once.
  4. Repeat for an \(11 \times 11\) grid of \((pc_{1}, pc_{2})\) and compare each inferred network with the true one using TPR and FPR.

docs.title: The network and the data¶
docs.text:
The network is a chain of 4 nodes, \(1-2-3-4\) (Fig. 2a of the paper). Each node is a logistic map, \(f(x) = r x (1 - x)\) with \(r = 4\), coupled as in Eq. (13):

\[ x^i_{n+1} = (1 - \alpha) f(x^i_n) + \frac{\alpha}{k_i} \sum_{j=1}^{N} A_{ij} f(x^j_n), \qquad \alpha = 0.1 . \]

docs.title: Amplitude correlation and phase synchronisation¶
docs.text:
Table 1 of the paper describes this system with the mean Pearson correlation of the pairs (about 0.05) and the Kuramoto order parameter \(\rho\) of the Hilbert phases (0.93). Correlation is weak but the phases are strongly synchronised.

To reproduce these numbers we pass demean=False to hilbert_phases, as the paper computed the phases of the raw signals. The maps take values in \([0, 1]\), and the Hilbert phase of a signal with a nonzero mean hardly moves, so part of this synchronisation is an artefact of the offset: with the library's default, demean=True, the order parameter is much lower.

docs.title: Pearson correlation cannot find the network, MIR can¶
docs.text:
In a bar plot of the pairs, a grey band between the connected pairs (purple) and the unconnected pairs (blue) means some threshold would separate them perfectly.

For Pearson correlation there is no such band (Fig. 2b): the indirect pairs 1–3 and 2–4 are more correlated than the direct pairs 1–2 and 3–4.

docs.title: One APMSD test: (pc₁, pc₂) = (0, 60)%¶
docs.text:
The paper shows this pair in Fig. 2c and Table 2: the amplitudes are kept and 60% of the phases are randomised. A significance level \(p_{sl} = 0.1\) means \(\aleph_{SD} = 1/p_{sl} = 10\) surrogates per pair, as in the paper.

mir_surrogate_test computes the MIR of the data and of every surrogate, the \(p\)-values and the FDR correction, and returns the inferred network. Given the true network, it also returns TPR and FPR.

docs.title: Comparison with Table 2 of the paper¶
docs.text: The table puts our values next to the paper's, for the original data and the mean over the 10 surrogates. The data and the surrogates are random, so the numbers agree to about two significant figures rather than exactly.

docs.title: The \((pc_{1}, pc_{2})\) parameter space¶
docs.text: Now repeat the test on the \(11 \times 11\) grid \(pc_{1}, pc_{2} \in \{0, 10, \dots, 100\}\%\) (Fig. 2d). Each point needs the MIR of 10 surrogates; the whole grid takes a few minutes.

docs.title: Choosing the best pair¶
docs.text: With a known network, the paper picks the pair whose (TPR, FPR) point is closest to perfect inference, \((1, 0)\), on the ROC plane: \(\tilde d = \sqrt{(1 - \mathrm{TPR})^2 + \mathrm{FPR}^2}\). Here many pairs reach \(\tilde d = 0\), so the first one found is reported.

docs.title: Down-sampling (Fig. 3)¶
docs.text: The paper also asks how few data points the method needs. If the \(10^5\) points were recorded over 10 seconds, the sampling rate is 10 kHz. Keeping every 100th point gives a 100 Hz recording of 1000 points, and every 500th point a 20 Hz recording of 200 points.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• MIR finds the structure of this network where Pearson correlation fails.
  • APMSD surrogates replace the threshold with a hypothesis test: at \((pc_{1}, pc_{2}) = (0, 60)\%\) the test recovers the chain exactly, as in the paper.
  • The parameter space shows which mix of amplitude and phase randomisation removes the dependence between linked nodes. Here phase randomisation is what matters, which fits the strong phase synchronisation (\(\rho \approx 0.93\)) and weak correlation of this system.
  • The method still works on down-sampled data of 1000 points; at 200 points this implementation does not reproduce the paper's Fig. 3c.

The functions used are documented in the Network Inference, Surrogate Data and Synchronisation API pages.

docs.title: References¶
docs.text: 1. H. Yıldırım and C. G. Antonopoulos, Network inference using mutual information rate, statistical tests and amplitude-phase modulated surrogate data, Chaos, Solitons & Fractals 188, 115554 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chaos.2024.115554

def simulate_oscillators(w, C_phase, C_amp, n_points=20_000, dt=0.01, sample_every=25,
                         n_transient=50_000, K=0.5, k=0.5, sigma_phase=0.1, tau=10.0,
                         sigma_amp=0.5, rng=None):
    # Signals x_i = a_i cos(theta_i) with separate phase (C_phase) and amplitude (C_amp) coupling.
    # C[i, j] = 1 means node i is driven by node j. Returns x, a and theta, each (n_points, n_nodes).
    rng = np.random.default_rng(rng)
    w = np.asarray(w, dtype=float)
    n = len(w)
    theta = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n)   # random initial phases
    loga = np.zeros(n)                     # initial amplitudes a_i = 1
    x_theta = np.empty((n_points, n))
    x_loga = np.empty((n_points, n))
    noise_phase = sigma_phase * np.sqrt(dt)
    noise_amp = sigma_amp * np.sqrt(2 * dt / tau)
    kept = 0
    for step in range(n_transient + n_points * sample_every):
        # deterministic parts of the two equations
        dtheta = w + K * (C_phase * np.sin(theta[None, :] - theta[:, None])).sum(axis=1)
        dloga = -loga / tau + k * (C_amp * (loga[None, :] - loga[:, None])).sum(axis=1)
        # Euler-Maruyama step
        theta = theta + dtheta * dt + noise_phase * rng.standard_normal(n)
        loga = loga + dloga * dt + noise_amp * rng.standard_normal(n)
        if step >= n_transient and (step - n_transient) % sample_every == 0:
            x_theta[kept], x_loga[kept] = theta, loga
            kept += 1
    a = np.exp(x_loga)
    return a * np.cos(x_theta), a, x_theta

def apmsd_grid(data, true_network, levels=LEVELS, rng=0):
    # Run the APMSD hypothesis test in every cell of the (p_c1, p_c2) grid.
    # Returns found[i, j, pair] (True where the pair is inferred as a link), TPR and FPR.
    rng = np.random.default_rng(rng)
    pairs = list(combinations(range(len(true_network)), 2))
    found = np.zeros((len(levels), len(levels), len(pairs)), dtype=bool)

    fpr = np.zeros((len(levels), len(levels)))

This is the main result of the tutorial:

  • the phase link D–P is detected in a vertical band: once enough phases are randomised (\(p_{c2}\) large), whatever happens to the amplitudes;
  • the amplitude link D–M is detected in a horizontal band: only when almost all amplitudes are randomised (\(p_{c1} \ge 90\%\)), whatever happens to the phases;
  • the unlinked pairs are never (or almost never) detected;
  • perfect inference happens only where the two bands overlap, the top-right corner.

So the position of the good cells tells us how the nodes are coupled. A surrogate can only reveal a link if it destroys the channel that carries it.

Note that the two axes are not on the same scale: the amplitude link needs almost all amplitudes randomised, the phase link a much smaller share of the phases. The amplitude changes slowly (\(\tau = 10\) time units, about 40 points), so the amplitudes left untouched between randomised points still carry most of the correlation, whereas a single random phase changes the sign of the signal.

docs.title: Phase and Amplitude Coupling in APMSD¶
docs.text:
In the previous tutorial we inferred a network with the mutual information rate (MIR) and amplitude-phase modulated surrogate data (APMSD), following Yıldırım & Antonopoulos [1]. The method replaces a fraction \(p_{c1}\) of the instantaneous amplitudes and a fraction \(p_{c2}\) of the instantaneous phases of every signal by random values, and calls a pair of nodes connected when the MIR of the data is higher than the MIR of its surrogates. The pairs \((p_{c1}, p_{c2})\) that give perfect inference change from one system to another: in the paper they lie at \(p_{c2} = 100\%\) for the stochastic Kuramoto oscillators (Section 3.4.3) but at small \(p_{c2}\) for the logistic maps.

Why? In this tutorial we test a simple explanation: the good cells depend on the channel through which the nodes interact. A pair of nodes can share its phase (the oscillations happen at the same time), its amplitude (the oscillations grow and shrink together), or both. To check this we build a toy model in which every link can be switched on in the phase only or in the amplitude only, something no real system allows.

You will learn:

  1. how to simulate oscillators whose phase and amplitude are coupled separately;
  2. how to measure phase and amplitude relations between pairs with the Hilbert transform;
  3. what the APMSD surrogates do to a signal;
  4. where in the \((p_{c1}, p_{c2})\) plane a phase link and an amplitude link are detected;
  5. what happens in a network that mixes both kinds of link, and why indirect pairs are a problem.

Running the whole notebook takes about 2–3 minutes on a laptop.

docs.title: 1. The model: oscillators with separate phase and amplitude¶
docs.text:
Each node \(i\) is a noisy oscillator,

\[ x_i(t) = a_i(t) \cos\theta_i(t), \]

whose phase \(\theta_i(t)\) and amplitude \(a_i(t) > 0\) are two separate random processes. The phase follows a noisy Kuramoto equation (Eq. (11) of the paper, with noise), and the logarithm of the amplitude, \(\ell_i = \log a_i\), an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process:

\[ d\theta_i = \Big(\omega_i + K \sum_j C^{\theta}_{ij} \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i)\Big)\,dt + \sigma_\theta\, dW_i, \]

\[ d\ell_i = \Big(-\frac{\ell_i}{\tau} + k \sum_j C^{a}_{ij} \big(\ell_j - \ell_i\big)\Big)\,dt + \sigma_a \sqrt{2/\tau}\; dV_i . \]

  • \(\omega_i\) is the natural frequency of node \(i\), and \(\sigma_\theta\) the strength of its phase noise.
  • \(C^{\theta}_{ij} = 1\) means node \(i\) is pulled towards the phase of node \(j\), with strength \(K\).
  • \(\tau\) is how long the amplitude remembers its past, and \(\sigma_a\) how much \(\ell_i\) fluctuates when the node is not coupled.
  • \(C^{a}_{ij} = 1\) means node \(i\) is pulled towards the amplitude of node \(j\), with strength \(k\).
  • \(W_i\) and \(V_i\) are independent Wiener processes (white noise).

Because the phase and the amplitude of every node are driven by independent noises and coupled through separate matrices, a link in \(C^{\theta}\) creates a relation between two phases and none between the amplitudes, and a link in \(C^{a}\) the opposite. We use the logarithm of the amplitude so that \(a_i = e^{\ell_i}\) stays positive.

We integrate the equations with the Euler–Maruyama method, the stochastic version of Euler's method: at every step \(\Delta t\) each deterministic term is multiplied by \(\Delta t\) and each noise term by \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\) times a standard normal random number,

\[ \theta_i \leftarrow \theta_i + \Big(\omega_i + K \sum_j C^{\theta}_{ij} \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i)\Big)\Delta t + \sigma_\theta \sqrt{\Delta t}\,\xi_i, \qquad \ell_i \leftarrow \ell_i + \Big(-\frac{\ell_i}{\tau} + k \sum_j C^{a}_{ij}(\ell_j - \ell_i)\Big)\Delta t + \sigma_a\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta t}{\tau}}\,\eta_i . \]

We use \(\Delta t = 0.01\), drop the first \(5 \times 10^4\) steps as a transient, and then keep one point every 25 steps (every 0.25 time units, about 25 points per oscillation) until we have \(L = 2 \times 10^4\) points.

docs.title: 2. A driver, a phase follower and an amplitude follower¶
docs.text:
We start with four nodes:

node frequency \(\omega\) phase amplitude D, driver 1.00 free free P, phase follower 1.10 pulled towards D's phase free M, amplitude follower 0.90 free pulled towards D's amplitude C, control 1.05 free free

So the true links are D–P (phase only) and D–M (amplitude only). P and M are not linked: P copies D's phase and M copies D's amplitude, so they have nothing in common. The coupling here is one-way (D drives, P and M follow), which is why only one entry of each matrix is set.

docs.title: 3. Measuring phase and amplitude relations from the data¶
docs.text:
In practice we only see the signals \(x_i(t)\), not \(\theta_i\) and \(a_i\). APMSD recovers an amplitude and a phase from each signal with the Hilbert transform \(\mathcal{H}\), which builds the analytic signal

\[ z_i(t) = x_i(t) + i\,\mathcal{H}[x_i](t) = A_i(t)\, e^{i \phi_i(t)} , \]

with instantaneous amplitude \(A_i = |z_i|\) and phase \(\phi_i = \arg z_i\). For a narrow-band oscillation like ours, \(A_i \approx a_i\) and \(\phi_i \approx \theta_i\).

From these we measure two relations for every pair:

  • the phase-locking value, \(\mathrm{PLV}_{ij} = \left|\langle e^{i(\phi_i - \phi_j)}\rangle_t\right|\) (the pairwise phase synchronisation of Eq. (16) in the paper): 1 for locked phases, near 0 for independent ones;
  • the amplitude correlation: Pearson's correlation between \(A_i(t)\) and \(A_j(t)\).

Remove the mean first. The Hilbert transform of a constant is zero, so a signal with a large mean \(\mu\) gives \(z(t) = \mu + (\text{small oscillation})\): its phase hovers around 0 for every node, and every pair looks phase-locked even when the nodes are not coupled at all. Our signals have mean close to zero, but for data such as the logistic map (values in \([0, 1]\)) subtracting each node's mean before the transform is essential.

docs.title: 4. What the APMSD surrogates do to a signal¶
docs.text:
To build a surrogate, cnd.amplitude_phase_surrogates takes the Hilbert amplitude and phase of every node, replaces a random fraction \(p_{c1}\) of the amplitudes by random values between the smallest and largest amplitude, and a random fraction \(p_{c2}\) of the phases by random values between the smallest and largest phase, and returns the real part, \(A\cos\phi\). The plot shows the driver's signal (black) and one surrogate (orange) in four cells:

  • at \((0, 0)\%\) nothing is changed, so the surrogate equals the data;
  • at \((100, 0)\%\) the phases are kept, so the surrogate still oscillates in step with the data, but its size is random at every point: the amplitude relation with other nodes is destroyed;
  • at \((0, 100)\%\) the amplitudes are kept but the phase is random at every point, so the oscillation, and with it any phase relation, is lost.

docs.title: 5. Where is each link detected?¶
docs.text: Now we run the full method of the paper over the \(11 \times 11\) grid of \((p_{c1}, p_{c2})\), with 10 surrogates per cell (\(p_{sl} = 0.1\)), using cnd.mir_surrogate_test. For every cell we keep the inferred network, so we can see in which cells each pair is called a link, as well as the TPR and FPR.

docs.title: 6. A network with phase links and amplitude links¶
docs.text:
Can one network have some links through the phase and others through the amplitude? In our model, yes: we only need to put them in different matrices. We build eight nodes with mutual coupling (\(C_{ij} = C_{ji}\)):

  • phase links: 1–2, 2–3, 5–6;
  • amplitude links: 3–4, 4–5, 6–7;
  • a link through both: 7–8.

Node 3 takes part in both kinds of link (phase with 2, amplitude with 4). The chains 1–2–3 (phase), 3–4–5 and 6–7–8 (amplitude) will also create indirect relations: 1 and 3 are both locked to 2, so they are locked to each other, even though they are not linked.

docs.title: 7. Removing indirect pairs with partial correlation¶
docs.text:
An indirect pair is related only through a third node. A partial correlation measures the relation between two nodes after removing what all the other nodes explain; it can be computed from the inverse of the covariance matrix \(P = \Sigma^{-1}\) as \(\rho_{ij \cdot \text{rest}} = -P_{ij} / \sqrt{P_{ii} P_{jj}}\).

We compute it in each channel separately:

  • for the amplitude, on the logarithm of the Hilbert amplitudes;
  • for the phase, on the short-time fluctuations of the phase: the unwrapped Hilbert phase minus its moving average over 40 points (10 time units). We cannot use the phases themselves, because the three nodes of a locked chain are all locked to each other.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• APMSD destroys the amplitude relations between nodes with \(p_{c1}\) and the phase relations with \(p_{c2}\). A link is detected only when the channel that carries it is destroyed: phase links appear in a vertical band, amplitude links in a horizontal band.
  • In a network that mixes both kinds of link, the whole network is found only where the bands overlap, so the location of the good cells reflects how the nodes are coupled.
  • Pairs that share a channel through a common neighbour behave exactly like links in every cell. Partial correlations, computed in the right channel, can remove them.

docs.title: Try it yourself¶
docs.text:
• Make the coupling weaker (K=0.2 or k=0.2 in simulate_oscillators): do the bands move or shrink?
  • Change the memory of the amplitude, tau. Does the amplitude band start at a smaller \(p_{c1}\) when the amplitude changes faster?
  • Couple M to D through both channels. Which band does the D–M link follow?
  • Use a shorter time series (n_points=5_000) and see which links are lost first.
